“The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = “with”) the trends of life… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, “that which co-exists with hita [welfare]”. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, “Art for artʼs sake,” cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement “Art for artʼs sake” is not acceptable; rather we should say, “Art for service and blessedness.”… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

The range and scope of short stories are exactly the same as those of plays, but short-story writers must know the technique of presenting a long story concisely. Suspense is equally effective in short stories as in plays; dramatic skill is essential for the writer of those short stories which come in the category of sketches, because a sketch holds an intermediate position between a story and a play.”

In the unique and superb interpretation of sáhitya, literature, in terms of “Art for service and blessedness” given above, the author has provided eternal guidance to all those related to the world of literature. With the basic objectives set by the author, literature with all its branches, including plays and short stories, can truly build up an ideal and just society, which is the demand of the day.

Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“The Practice of Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted from above. But he did not stop there. Advancing further, he translated his words into actions, creating a direct example in the form of his own literature, marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus we get a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part set was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that we are extremely happy to present to the readers now Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast domain of linguistics and philology which touched also on history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books. Apart from the books mentioned above, some stories are from a volume of the authorʼs childrenʼs literature series – namely, In the Land of Hat́t́amálá.
In the interest of accuracy, the authorʼs explanations of certain Sanskrit, Bengali and other terminologies have all been retained in full.
Source references for all material in the book are provided at the end of this publisherʼs note.
Footnotes by the translators have all been signed “–Trans.” Unsigned footnotes are those of the author.

Many readers are concerned that the authorʼs discourses, as published, should adhere as closely as possible to the precise wording the author used in speaking. For this reason, in the case of discourses given originally in English, the editors do not alter pronouns and other terms which the author in his lifetime considered “common-gender” words. As the author once said, “You know, ‘man’ is not only masculine gender, ‘man’ is common gender also. ‘Man is mortal’ – here ‘man’ means both male and female.”

The author was a natural advocate of womenʼs rights and on at least one occasion indicated that “lopsided justice” in language should be eliminated at some future date. In keeping with his guideline and with current trends, it is our policy in the case of translated discourses (where the published wording will necessarily be that of the translators) to use gender-neutral language.

Square brackets [ ] in the text are used to indicate translations by the editors or other editorial insertions. Round brackets ( ) indicate a word or words originally given by the author. When round brackets follow an English word or phrase and contain the equivalent Bengali word or phrase, it should be understood that the English words represent the English translation, while the contents of the brackets are the original Bengali words provided as extra information for the reader.

The author used a particular shorthand for explaining the etymologies of words. Under this system, a minus sign (–) follows a prefix, and a plus sign (+) precedes a suffix. Thus ava – tr + ghaiṋ = avatára can be read, “the root tr prefixed by ava and suffixed by ghaiṋ becomes avatára.”

Human beings look for comfort. Thus the etymological meaning of the word d́ha that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root d́huńd́a, is “instrument of pleasure”; colloquially, it is called gadi [mattress or cushion]. Therefore gadi means “something which makes our lying or sitting comfortable”. The word d́ha can be used for the kind of cushion that we use under the mattress of a cot or the cushion that we use on a chair.
chapterTitle: Who is Looking after the Office?

t: In North India, the word gaddá is generally used. But that does not mean that the word gaddii is not in use. However, in North and West India gaddii means “the place where the shopkeeper sits and looks after the office work or the accounts”; that is, the office. The office of various business enterprises is also called gaddii. The use of the word gaddii reminds me of the story of a merchant.
chapterTitle: Who is Looking after the Office?

t: Sethjii [the merchant] was critically ill; he was on his death bed and the house was full of loud lamentation. On hearing the news of his imminent death the creditors became anxious. The debtors of Sethjii, on the other hand, had a slight glow on their faces, like the film of a thin cream of diluted milk. The children of Sethjii were terribly busy managing the matters related to the accounts of sales-tax, income-tax, excise-duty, and so on.
chapterTitle: Who is Looking after the Office?

t: When Sethjii was about to breathe his last, all his seven children closed the gaddii [office] and stood by his death bed with folded hands. Sethjii started enquiring about their welfare by naming each of them. First he enquired about his eldest son. Sethjii asked, “Is Ramnajar present?” Ramnajar answered with folded hands, “Yes father, I am present”. Then he looked for the second son and asked, “Is Rampariikśań present?” Rampariikśań replied, “Yes, father, I am present.” Next he asked about the third son, “Is Ramsurath present?” Ramsurath responded, “Yes father, I am standing at your lotus feet”. Then Sethjii wanted to know about the fourth son, and asked, “Is Ramsiḿhásan present?” Ramsiḿhásan replied, “Yes father, your servant is present”. Then he enquired about the fifth son, “Is, Ramikbal present?” Ramikbal replied, “Yes father, I am standing at your feet.” Then he asked about the sixth son, “Is Rambeshan present?” Rambeshan answered, “Yes father, your servant is present”. Next he looked for the seventh son and asked, “Is Rananut́há present?” Rananut́há replied, “Your servant is here at your service.” Then the Sethjii flew into a rage and thundered, “If all seven brothers are present here then who is on the gaddii [who is looking after the office]?” As Sethjii started fuming and shouting his heart stopped and he died.
chapterTitle: Who is Looking after the Office?

t: So, now you understand that Bengali gadi [cushion] and gaddii [the office] in North India are not the same thing. Do not mix up the two.
chapterTitle: Who is Looking after the Office?

t: One who knows neither Hindi nor English may, on hearing Hindi, take it to be English. Also, on hearing English they may think it to be Hindi. The same kind of confusion may take place in relation to gadi and gaddii in Bengali and Hindi, respectively. When somebody says, Málik gaddii me háiṋ [The owner is in the office], a Bengali may take it to mean that the owner has been lying on the mattress of his bed. On the other hand, when a Bengali says, “Málik gadite shuye áche.” [The owner is sleeping on a mattress], someone who does not know Bengali may think that the owner is possibly lying on a bed in his shop.

Perhaps you do not know this story. Once, a rabid advocate of the national language arrived at Patna station. He was to go to the Patna secretariat but he would not use the word “secretariat” because it was English. In fact, he would not even use the word “English”. So, at the station he asked the rickshaw puller, “Please take me to the saciválay [secretariat]. The rikshaw puller was also a great lover of the national language [Hindi]! He at once retorted, “What, sáhab [sir], why are you saying saciválay, saciválay in English? Please speak in Hindi. I donʼt understand English.”

The lover of the national language was in a fix. He then tried to explain in a roundabout way, “Saciválay jii [O man] saciválay, which some people by mistake call ‘secretariat’ (he wouldnʼt speak English either).
The rickshaw puller said, “Thatʼs what you should say. Say it in Hindi – ‘secretariat’. Why are you saying saciválay, saciválay in English?”
The problem of the great lover of the national language was finally solved. He felt as though he were holding the full moon in his hand.

A boy of Munghyer district went to Patna to study his M. A. in Hindi. The language of his home was Auṋgiká, the language of his village was Auṋgiká and the language of his district was also Auṋgiká. The language of his umbilical cord [his mother tongue] was Auṋgiká. The language of his kitchen was Auṋgiká, the language of his house [the language of conversation of the inmates of the house] was Auṋgiká. After going to Patna, by conversing with his teachers and classmates, he had developed a good proficiency in Hindi. He also used to take part in Hindi plays. Then, during the summer holidays he came home. At noon he told his mother [in refined Hindi], “Mátah, myáṋy kśudhárta huṋ. Mujhe anna dená” [Mother, I am hungry; please give me some food].
Mother said, “Kii nunnu, kii balaechi. Hamma nay samajhaychia. Hámrá ráḿrejii nay ávaeche” [My child, what are you saying? I canʼt understand. I donʼt know English].
Smilingly, the son said in Auṋgiká, “Hege, máy! Bhukh lágloche, kháyla deba” [Oh mother, I feel hungry, will you give me something to eat?]
The mother then said, “Háṋ nunnu, háṋ nunnu, deyachia, deyachia” [Yes, my child, I am just about to give you some food].

The word d́hekur is derived from the word d́hekkar which means “to burp”. Sometimes the extravagance of intelligence is also described as d́hekure buddhi [burping intelligence]. Humans with d́hekure buddhi are intelligent but they cannot always maintain their balance. Luckily, the number of people with burping intelligence is always very small in every age and in every country. Yet, sometimes even these people with such intelligence do wonderful jobs. However, it is difficult to say whether this is due to the quality of their intelligence or just a fluke.
Once I heard the story of a man with burping intelligence. He was matchless in managing a situation or solving problems.

An oath-taking ceremony of ministers was to take place in some country of the world. It was to be held in the durbar ( 1 ) of the Governor of that place. The entire responsibility of supervising the ceremony was on the shoulders of this man with burping intelligence. The prospective ministers kept sitting with their heads tilted to one side, impatiently waiting for the auspicious moment of the oath-taking. They looked like those pots of date palm raw sugar kept on biṋd́e ( 2 ).They had donned new clothes, some had a mark of sandalwood paste on their foreheads and some had put marks of curd on their foreheads. Those who swaggered about as atheists did not put any mark on their forehead out of shyness, but hid a sanctified flower in their chest pockets and silently kept on chanting the name of their respective cherished deities, which “nobody will know about, nobody will hear.”
All eyes were glued on the man with burping intelligence (dhekure buddhimán). One prospective minister had started weeping. He was saying, “For Godʼs sake, sir, please donʼt make me a minister!”

The d́hekure buddhimán said, “Why are you so worried? Just see, so many prospective ministers are sitting, immaculately dressed. It is strange that you are crying on this auspicious day!” He took out a handkerchief from his pocket and wiped the tears of the unwilling prospective minister, but his crying would not stop. Sometimes he was weeping, sometimes he was crying breathlessly.

Then the d́hekure buddhimán addressed the prospective ministers and said, “I hope you understand the difference between an assembly and a council.” Some said, “Yes, I do” and some said, “No, I donʼt.”
The d́hekure buddhimán said, “I will so meticulously explain everything that you wonʼt have any problem in future, because ultimately my promotion depends entirely on your grace.”
He continued, “Do you know who is called an MLA or an MP?” Some said, “Yes, I do”; some said, “No, I donʼt”.
The d́hekure buddhimán said, “I will explain it to you. Since it is an important matter you should thoroughly understand it.”

“Now, what happened was, a minister who did not know any English mistook MLA for an indigenous word and took the word to be eme le. You know that what is called is me [in something] in Hindi and er madhye in Bengali is called eme in the language of Bihar, and the word le simply means ”take“. The minister thought, eme le means ‘take in it’. That means, whatever you find, on any side – to your front or behind you, on the right or on the left, offered in gestures, in kind or cash, in this thing or that – just put it in your pocket. As the minister did not know the exact meaning of MLA he made his pocket so heavy that finally wicked people started accusing him of taking bribes. A mischievous commission also found him guilty of taking bribes. At last the minister lost his job. Anyway, please learn the exact meaning of MLA in advance. Donʼt pronounce it eme le.”

The prospective ministers said, “Yes, we certainly understand! We donʼt make such mistakes.” The reluctant prospective minister said, “I donʼt need to know all those things because I donʼt want to become a minister at all.”

Then the d́hekure buddhimán told the prospective ministers, “In case you have to sneeze or cough, please get it over with, quickly. The Governor will be arriving any moment now. If anybody has to go to the bathroom or toilet I request him to do it quickly.”

The prospective ministers again sat down smartly after tidying their clothes. The reluctant prospective minister said, “I donʼt need to sneeze or cough or go to the bathroom. Please donʼt make me a minister.”

The d́hekure buddhimán further told the prospective ministers, “When you are going to the bathroom you can also use some perfume or put a cotton pad soaked in áttar [flower essence] into your ears because if the Governor expresses a desire to have a photograph taken with you, then the perfume on your body will emit a fine fragrance. Well, now let me teach you the regulations of protocol. Always assume a modesty of bearing, whether that modesty is needed or not. When you are served refreshments, donʼt start gobbling them up. However much temptation you may feel, you must resist it and eat slowly. If there is a salted snack on the plate, bite it in such a way that only a third of it goes into your mouth and two thirds are left behind. Again, if there are sweets on the plate, bite in such a way that only one fourth enters your mouth and three fourths are left behind on the plate. If you take tea or coffee, first pour it into a saucer and drink only half of it, leaving the rest on the saucer. Then, drink straight from the cup but you must stop as soon as you have finished half the cup, and leave the other half of the drink in the cup itself. After that, if you feel hungry you can take a bellyful of muŕi-begunpoŕá [parched rice and burnt brinjal] after returning home. If the Governor wonders, “Whatʼs the matter? You are not taking the refreshments. Is the food not palatable?” You will answer, “No, sir, the food is very good. It is actually our fault, because, always busy and engrossed in the thoughts of the welfare of the country as we are, we never get time to have refreshments. Not taking any refreshments for days on has become such a bad habit that we are now not able to consume even this delicious food.”
Weeping, the reluctant prospective minister said, “If Iʼm given any refreshments I wonʼt touch them.”

“Yes, one more word”, said the d́hekure buddhimán, “In whatever language the Governor asks you something, you must use very few words in reply, flashing just a sweet smile. That will give the Governor an impression that you have understood his words. And if in fact you donʼt understand, I am here to explain everything to you. I will also write letters for you, correcting the mistakes. I shall draft the letter too; you donʼt have to worry. You will just sign at the bottom.”
The d́hekure buddhimán asked the prospective ministers, “Do all of you know how to sign?”
Most of the prospective ministers said, “Yes, we know.”
A very few said, “We canʼt sign but we know how to give our thumbprint.”
One said, “I have given my thumbprint many times but I canʼt remember at the moment whether I should use the big toe of my right foot or left foot”.
The d́hekure buddhimán said, “I shall explain everything to you in the minutest details, you donʼt have to worry at all.”
Around this time, all of a sudden the Governor arrived with his retinue. The first thing that came to his notice was the reluctant prospective minister lying down on the floor.

The Governor asked him, “On such an auspicious day, on such a joyous occasion, why are you lying on the floor, covered with dust?” The reluctant prospective minister burst out crying, “I donʼt want to become a minister, sir. (Crying at a higher pitch.) Donʼt make me a minister, sir. (Crying at a still higher pitch.) I beseech you, sir, please donʼt make me a minister!”
The Governor said, “But why, why are you so reluctant to become a minister?”

The reluctant prospective minister said, “To be a minister one has to suffer a lot of trouble. Suppose, I have decided to go somewhere, I have packed my luggage and then, on account of some unavoidable reason, I have to postpone my journey. Suppose, I have given my final word to somebody that I would meet him, and the gentleman comes to see me. But then for an unavoidable reason I have to postpone the meeting. I have heard that occasionally one has even to die for an unavoidable reason. The most terrible thing that I have heard is that sometimes, even after death, the news of the death has to be kept suppressed for unavoidable reason. In other words, one has to remain bási maŕá [dead overnight]. You know, sir, many people do not like to remain dead overnight. They consider it as something undesirable. You know, there is a story about it.

Rama was performing the ashavamedha yajiṋa [the horse sacrifice]. The two brothers Lab and Kush stopped the yajiṋa horse while staying in the hermitage of the saint Valmiki. Rama came to Lab and Kush and requested them to release the horse. Lab and Kush asked Rama, “Whatʼs the name of your father”? Ram replied, “Dasharath”. Lab and Kush asked, “Which Dasharath is that? We have heard of only one Dasharath.”
Ek dasharather kathá jáni agágoŕá,
Cari putra thákite ye holo bási maŕá.
[We know the entire story of one Dasharath who, in spite of having four sons, died overnight].]
“So, my lord Governor, I donʼt want to become ‘dead overnight’ for unavoidable reason. I must fervently request you not to make me a minister. Please donʼt make me a minister.”
Then, making their voices as sweet and sympathetic as possible, the Governor and the d́hekure buddhimán asked him, “If you donʼt want to become a minister at all, why have you come here, then?”

The reluctant prospective minister said, “I have not come here on my own, sir. I was called to repair the electric wires of this hall. I have finished my work and now I want to leave, sir. I have not come here to become a minister, sir. I am not an MLA, sir. I am only an electrician. For Godʼs sake, donʼt make me a minister by force, sir.”

Wearing a sweet smile on their lips the Governor and the d́hekure buddhimán said, “When you donʼt want to become a minister by any means, when you want to leave, you can go. We shall not force you to stay here. But it would have been better had you taken the oath of ministry before leaving. Such a rare opportunity does not come in oneʼs life time and again.”
Anyway, you have now heard the story of the d́hekure buddhimán.

The greatest king of the Gupta dynasty was Samudragupta. But the name that immediately comes to the mind when we talk about the Gupta period is Chandragupta. Although Samudragupta became famous as a great conqueror, had established a huge empire in India and brought about a great change in the cultural life of the people, it was Chandragupta who was the fire brand hero of the Gupta era. His love for his subjects was legendary. It was due to his inspiration and efforts that the Sanskrit language got new life.

While talking about Chandragupta, I remember a funny story. In Bengal there is a village named Káliá. The villagers are highly educated. It is doubtful whether there is another such village in the world. Close to Káliá is situated the village of Bádiá. The villagers of that village are also well-educated. Once, the boys of Káliá were planning to stage the play Chandragupta on some festive occasion and the search was on for suitable actors and actresses for the various roles. Around that time, a stranger, whose name was possibly Dashamikranjan Dasgupta, came from a distant village. He looked like a storm-ruffled crow or a messenger from the battle field. He said, “Wonʼt you give me a part?”
The organisers asked, “What kind of part do you want?”

Dashamik replied, Kyábol rájár párt́ karmu. Syánápati kimbá sakár-napharer párt́ karmu ná. Kon nát́ak aityáse? [I shall only play the part of a king. I shall not do the part of the general or the servants or menials. Which play are you going to stage?].
The organisers said, “We are going to stage Chandragupta. In this play there are two kings – Chandragupta and Alexander.”
Dashamik said, Áleksándár námd́á ussárań kará shakta. Ámáre sandragupta dyábáni? [It is difficult to pronounce the name ‘Alexander’. Canʼt you give me the part of Chandragupta?]
The organisers said, “Very well, that will be done. Will you be able to play the part?”
Dashamik said, “Of course I can. If I canʼt, who else can? Just get me the script of the part. There is no need for rehearsals. I shall come straight to the stage and show what is meant by acting.”

The rehearsal was in full swing. The prompter asked the actor who was to play the part of Alexander, to say “Really, Selucas, how strange is this country!” Suddenly, Dashamik appeared from nowhere and said, “Let me ask you one thing. Of which country was Chandragupta the king?”
The organisers said, “Of Magadh.”
Dashamik asked, “Magadh! Is it bigger or smaller than our Káliá-Bádiá?”
The organisers said, “Look, our Káliá-Bádiá is just a village, and Magadh is a land, a big land in fact.”
Dashamik said, “I see. Then itʼs a good part.”
There was silence for a while. The prompter kept sitting silently. The actors and actresses also waited silently to hear what Dashamik was going to say next.
Dashamik said, “Chandragupta... Chandra Gupta... Chandra Gupta... Chandragupta. Well, is this Chandragupta a Sengupta or a Dasgupta?”
The organisers said, “Neither Sengupta nor Dasgupta, just Gupta.”

Dashamik said, “Only Gupta? Then he must be a low caste Vaedya. Only Guptas are low caste Vaedyas. So, I wonʼt do that part. No I wonʼt. No, I wonʼt by any means. Please give me the part of Alexander.

“What a beautiful part! Ah, ah! How sweet are the words, Haittoi chelukach, kii vicitra ei dyásh! Huinyá man-práń cital aiyá jáy.” [Really, Selucas, how strange is this country! The words are so soothing to my heart and mind!]

The meaning of the verbal root tan is “to grow, to be manifest”. The word ta that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root tan is used for “one who can express their ideas in music and dance”, and “acting and recitation”. So, in this case one of the meanings of the word ta is “an actor”. Sometimes an actor displays a strange presence of mind. In that sense he is a ta in both respects. There are many stories about the presence of mind or the nature of the presence of mind of these ta of the theatre world. I shall tell you one or two of such stories.

It was then the British period. I was at Dinajpur at that time. Like other towns of North Bengal, Dinajpur was also a decent middle class town. I liked the town very much. I particularly liked a special characteristic of the residents of Dinajpur. They [in Bengali, oṋŕá ( 1 ) ] were very fond of dancing, singing and acting.

In those days there was hardly any permanent theatrical stage outside Kolkata, but there was one at Dinajpur. Some of the local actors had already become quite eminent. Theatre was live and very popular, not only in towns but also in villages. At that time the play Sita had reached the zenith of its popularity. The actor who won accolades by playing the role of Sita was possibly Abdul Latif.

The play Sita was on. There was a big crowd of thousands of bullock carts in the town. All the villagers had come to see the performance. They had a lot of money on them from selling jute, and were prepared to spend lavishly if necessary, to see the theatre.

The play was on. The action had reached its climax. Now Sita was to enter the earth. In brief, Sita was supposed to say, addressing the earth, “Oh mother earth, split open so that I can take a place in your lap.” Abdul Latif knew the drift of the play very well and he remembered most of the dialogues by heart. He also knew how he was to address mother earth at this point. But he had some confusion about the exact language of the dialogue. At that critical moment after he had just said, “Oh mother earth”, the prompter had a sudden bout of coughing. On account of the attack of coughing he was not able to speak, but “Sita” could not keep on standing with his mouth shut, waiting for him. He applied his presence of mind and said in the local dialect, “Mátah basundhare tui pháṋk ha, mui bhitarat dhukim”. [Mother earth, split – I want to go inside].
I noticed that the audience accepted it as normal; it did not affect the aesthetics of the drama.

There should be thorough rehearsals for quite a few days before a play is staged. Various kinds of mannerisms of the actors and actresses (such as moving their hands and feet, some peculiar gestures and gesticulations, shaking the lips, turning the neck etc), defects of pronunciation (for example dyásh [for desh] kyábal [for kebal], onárá [for oṋŕá], cáikel [for sáikel], myágh [for megh], and malapropisms (mayávii in place of mayámay, nindak in place of ninduk) are easily detected during the rehearsals and can be rectified. It is therefore better not to believe those who say, “ekkere styáje áisyá dyaákhaiyá dimu ayáktiḿ káre kay” [Onstage, I shall show what acting really is]. It is better to have a thorough checking during the rehearsals.

Kusumkumari was a famous actress of that time. Her acting talents were simply superb but she would often be absent during rehearsals. This was the biggest problem with her. As a person Kusumkumari was very good and idealistic. The man of whom she was most fond had the surname “Biswas”, [meaning “faith”]. When this man surnamed Biswas died, Kusumkumari started eating only one meal a day as widows do. She would just have a simple vegetarian meal at noon. For financial reason she was obliged to continue acting but the rest of the time she used to wear a sari without a coloured border or edge [the usual dress of a widow].

Whatever may be, for some sound reason the word “Biswas” got fixed in Kusumkumariʼs mind. During the production of one play she came straight to the stage without attending the rehearsal even for a single day. She was to deliver the following dialogue: “Donʼt go to him, donʼt go to him; he exhales poison [nihshváse bis]”. She said, instead, with full-throated emotion, “Donʼt go to him. Donʼt go to him, donʼt go to him. There is nis in his biswás” [The humour lies in the spoonerism of saying biswáse nis in place of nihswáse bis].

In the past, the Oriya people living in Kolkata used to smoke a lot of guŕukii tobacco. The local people did not enjoy that particular kind of tobacco. A few who had developed a taste for it used to meet the Oriya people in secret and had a puff of guŕuk. Generally, the Oriyas are very good people. They cannot refuse anything to anybody. Therefore they used to satisfy the guŕuk lovers by giving them guŕukii tobacco. It is said that in some unknown scripture it is written:
Támrakútaḿ mahaddravyaḿ shraddhayá diiyate yadi,
Ashvamedhasamapuńyaḿ t́áne t́áne bhaviśyati.

This claims that tobacco is a great thing. If anybody offers it to somebody with respect, with every puff of the recipient, the giver of the tobacco acquires virtue equal to the virtue acquired by performing ashvamedha yajiṋa ( 1 ). Such was the reputation of the guŕukii tobacco of that time.

An open-air music drama based on the incidents of the life of Krśńa was on. The play had already gathered momentum. Everybody was all praise for the actor playing the part of Krśńa. The prompter was to say, “Oh Rádhá, please lift your face.” Just at that time the prompter had a sudden bout of coughing. He was not able to speak on account of the cough. But the seasoned actor who was playing the part of Krśńa could not remain silent at such a climactic dramatic moment. He felt fidgety about what to say. Just at that time a member of the concert party, while offering guŕukii tobacco to another member, said, “Come, my brother, have a puff of guŕuk.”
That solved the problem of the actor playing Krśńa. He felt like someone in remission of malarial fever. He said, “Oh Rádhá, please lift your face and have a puff of guŕuk.”

In the past, both in theatre and in open air musical drama, the organisers used to plant some of their own people here and there amongst the spectators. When the management wanted to make a particular actor or actress or a singer popular in a short time, these people used to call out “Encore! Encore!” from different parts of the auditorium, with or without reason. In keeping harmony with them other spectators also joined them in a chorus. Everybody thought, “They must be highly talented and that is probably why we hear the applause and ‘Encore! Encore!’.” Sometime later these planted admirers used to call out, “Dádá ghurre phirre” [Brother, play it elaborately], to the tune of bala hari hari bol [“Utter the name of Hari again and again” – the chant accompanying a Hindu funeral procession]. As a result of these happenings, the name and fame of the actors and actresses used to spread far and wide.

In our place there was a huge, hefty fellow named Pramatharanjan Bhattacharya. He was not very tall but he was unnaturally fat. As a result, he looked like a rectangle. People used to gaze at him for his lustrous beauty. Once, Pramatharanjan was given the part of Ghat́otkac in the play Kurukśetra. He was extremely intelligent. He felt that he was not given the proper training in the rehearsal, that he should say everything written in the script. The directions in the script regarding the death of Ghat́otkac were as follows: “Fall down and die”. So, while acting, at the time of falling down, Ghat́otkac announced quite dramatically, “Fall down and die!”. After that he fell flat on the stage.

Since that time, the theatre organizers became wary of him and were reluctant to give him any part, but where would they get such an extraordinary figure as his? So, the next time he was given the part of Bhiima. He asked, “I hope there is enough scope for dialogue in the role of Bhiima.” Everybody said, “You donʼt have to talk much because wielding the club on the stage is quite tiring, so just wield the club for a little while and then leave the stage.”

Pramatharanjan resented this, “Why should I wield the club only for a little while? Why should I not wield it for a long time? Let me tell you very frankly that if the spectators say ‘Encore! Encore!’ from one corner of the auditorium to the other, with applause, I shall wield the club for an hour, and if somebody says, 'Dádá ghurre phirreʼ ['Please swing it round and round, please do it elaboratelyʼ], then I shall even get down into the auditorium and wield the club in the midst of the crowd of spectators, at least for sometime.”

The organizers instructed their own people not to say “Encore! Encore!” or “Dádá ghurre phirre”, even by mistake. That was the arrangement. In the play Pramatharanjan had nothing to say in the role of Bhiima. He was only supposed to enter the stage at the point where there is an instruction, “Enter Bhiima with club in hand”, and leave the stage after wielding the club for a short while.

Pramatharanjan thought that the dramatist had lacked foresight. Had he had foresight he could have envisaged that one day a powerful figure like Pramatharanjan would appear in the role of Bhima in that play. In that case he would have written some powerful dialogue for Bhiima. However, Pramatharanjan was not a person to lose heart easily. He saw that in that part of the script was written, “Enter Bhiima with club in hand”. He thought, “Well, I must exploit this opportunity to settle my scores with the dramatist. If I say exactly what the dramatist has written then where is my special skill? Let me change it a little.” In due course of time, Pramatharanjan appeared on the stage with a club in his hand, and while violently wielding the club he kept on saying repeatedly, “Enter club with Bhima in hand.”

In the Bengal of those days, every educated person was familiar with the book Niiladarpańa. Dinabandhu Mitra wrote this book based on the British exploitation of the indigo planters who cultivated indigo. Although well educated, Dinabandhu Mitra used to mix with the common people and was quite familiar with their feelings and language. He was a close friend of Bankimchandra. Once he came to a village in Jessorre [a district in the former undivided Bengal, now in Bangladesh] to get an idea of the peopleʼs opinion regarding his Niiladarpańa. He was crossing the river in a boat owned by someone called Hafij Mian. From the discussion of the crew he understood that the play Niiladarpańa had been staged in their village the previous night. They were discussing only this. He asked Hafiz Mian, “Well, brother, how was the play?” He replied, “Oh sir, what can I say? It is simply excellent.”

Mr. Mitra again asked, “Was the dramatist able to properly express the feelings and language of the poor farmers?” Hafij said, “Does that need saying? While witnessing the play I had a feeling that the fellow had given an eyewitness account.” On hearing these remarks Dinabandhu Mitra felt a profound satisfaction.

One day, Niiladarpańa was being staged. Iswarchandra Vidyasagar was in the audience, which comprised many eminent people. There was a heartrending scene. An Englishman associated with the indigo plantation was torturing a humble indigo farmer. The cruelty of the Englishman and the helplessness of the farmer were eloquently evident through the actorsʼ portrayal. Vidyasagar could not stand the atrocities perpetrated on the farmer. He removed a Taltala sandal ( 1 ) from his foot and threw it at the Englishman.
The curtain fell.

After some time the curtain was lifted and Girish Ghosh appeared on the stage, carrying Vidyasagarʼs Taltala sandal on his head. He said, “During my entire acting career I have never received such a valuable reward for my acting. It has given a sense of fulfillment to our acting careers and to the theatre stage of Bengal as well. I request the honourable Vidyasagar to allow us to keep this sandal. For his use we have already sent someone to buy a pair of sandals from Taltala.”

An open-air musical drama was being staged in the village. Giitábhinay ( 1 ) was being performed in the vast grounds in front of the zamindarʼs [Land owner] house. Everybody, in addition to playing the role assigned to them, was trying to especially please the zamindar, to wangle an extra monetary reward from him. Such a practice was quite common in the Bengal of those days. Even those who did not have any elem ( 2 ) [real talent] managed to get some reward from the zemindar by flattering him. There runs a story:

A poetic duel between Bhola Mayra of Jara village and a certain Jagu Thakur was going on in the house of Madhusudan Banerjee, the village zamindar. Jagu Thakur saw that he was no match for Bhola Mayra. So, he decided to get some money by flattering the zamindar. Going beyond the scope of the musical drama, he started singing,
E ek Vrndávan re bhái e ek Vrndávan,
Hetháy baḿshii báján liila karen Shriimadhusudan.
[This is a veritable Vrindavan, my brother, this is a veritable Vrindavan. Here Shrii Madhusudhan, that is, Krśńa himself, plays the flute and performs his acts of dalliance.]
Bhola Mayra could not stand it. He at once rejoined:
Keman kare balli jagá jáŕá golok Vrndávan,
Hethá tulasii maiṋca kotháy peli savi dekhi báṋsher van.
Baḿshiidhvani shuńli kotháy ore masháy kare bhan bhan.
Kavi gábi paysá pábi ata khoshámader kii kárań.

[How do you say, Jagá, that this Jáŕá is the heavenly Vrindavan? Where do you see a basil altar here? I only see a bamboo grove. Where do you hear the melodious sound of a flute? It is full of buzzing mosquitoes. You will get money for your song. So, what is the point of so much flattery?]

The place I am talking about was staging a particular open-air musical drama named Lakśmańer Shaktishel [The powerful missile of Laksmana]. The job of Vivek [conscience, as a narrator] in an open-air musical drama is to give an idea, through songs, of the events which are happening or which are about to happen. But the person playing the role of Vivek in that particular place did not want to follow the beaten track. He wanted instead to antagonize the zamindar against Ravana and thereby elicit a reward.
Rávań ásila judde paiyá but́ jutá,
Hanumán máre táre láthi-sar–gutá.
Sar káiyá Rávań rájá jáy garágari,
Hanumán bale, 'tore máirási sápari.
Sápar márini tore máirási sápari,
Sápar márile tui jáitis jamer báriʼ.

[Ravana came to the battle field with shoes on and Hanuman started giving him kicks, slaps and pushes. On being slapped, Ravana the king started grovelling in the dust and Hanuman said, “I have given you only a gentle slap. I have not given you real slaps but only gentle slaps. Had I given you real slaps you would simply have died.”]

The zamindar was very happy. He at once called the treasurer and told him, “Give ten rupees to Vivek as a reward.” The man who was playing the role of Ravana was playing the part very sincerely and seriously. The clashes and clanking of weapons suggested his super-heroic grandeur. Rama was absolutely cornered out of fear, tension and anxiety; he could not utter a single word. It was an unbearable situation. The zamindar would not stand it. He said, “Cut off one of Ravanaʼs heads. How audacious! Ten-headed Ravana will become nine-headed from today.”

You know, in theatre productions, Ravana has, of course, only one real head and the other nine are false. The footmen of the zamindar cut off one of the false heads. Meanwhile, Ravana struck Laksman fatally with his most powerful missile.

Hanuman at once ran in search of mrtasaiṋjiivanii [the reviving herb] known as vishalyakarańii. There was joyous celebration in the camp of the rákśasas [demons], while in Ramaʼs camp there were loud lamentations and groaning cries. The zamindar could not bear it any longer. He said, “The scoundrel has not yet come to his senses. Chop off another of his heads. Ten-headed Ravana is today reduced to an eight-headed person.”

In the next scene, the tables were turned, as Ravana was facing defeat in the battle. He prayed intensely to Lord Shiva, “Oh Lord Shiva, You are one who is easily pleased. Whatever sins I might have committed, please remember that I am your son. Please have mercy on me. Without your mercy it is not possible to win; it is not possible to even survive.”

Ravana went on praying, ruefully shedding tears all the while. This sight evoked the zamindarʼs pity. He said, “The pitiable sight of Ravana makes me melt in sympathy. How sad! Re-affix the two heads and make him a ten-headed person once again.”

Medicine kills disease. That is why one of the etymological meanings of the word tha that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root thurva is “medicine”. In this sense, “medicine” does not refer only to diseases of the body but also to diseases to the mind. One medicine for mental disease is to lighten the mind by inducing pleasant feelings, the purpose being to remove tension and anxiety. This is the reason why in ancient times there used to be a kind of person who kept people happy by using different kinds of humour so that their minds overflowed with joy. These people might not have been very educated or scholarly but they were definitely experts in human psychology. These people were called jesters. Your must be quite familiar with the abstract noun, vaeduśya [jest].
Vak baekharii shabdajharii shástra vyákhyána kaoshalam,
Vaeduśyaḿ viduśaḿ tadvat bhuktaye na tu muktaye.

This means that whether a jester has scholarship or not, he must have a knowledge of psychology. He must also have a ready wit. Many of you must have heard the name of Sharat Chandra Pandit of Murshidabad. There have rarely been born jesters of his standard. Generally known as Dádát́hákur [elderly Brahmin] this man also ran a journal entitled Viduśaka [the jester]. Once, a conference of the Bengali Literature Association was held in Berhampur. Amongst the delegates present, Sharatchandra Pandit was of course there but there was also the famous litterateur, Sharatchandra Chattopadhyay, who was at that time at the height of his fame. His newly published novel The Libertine [Caritrahiin, meaning “a person of loose morals”] was selling like hot cakes [in Bengali, bejáy ( 1 ) kát́ti] fresh from the oven.

Sharatchandra was a great litterateur, no doubt, but he was not good at delivering lectures. In small circles, he was a maestro of gossip. People insisted that he should speak something in the conference. Sharatchandra somehow blurted out something and sat down. Before sitting he said, “I wonʼt say much here, it is the jester, Sharatchandra, who will speak at length”.
Sharat Chandra Pandit [Dádát́hákur] stood up, spoke for sometime and finally said, “My knowledge is very poor; that ‘libertine’ Sharatchandra is much more knowledgeable than I”.

While talking about the jester, I was reminded of the story of four brothers. What is more, as I am going to tell the story of the four brothers, the story of the four and a half brothers is also hovering in my mind. In ancient times, in a holy place in India, the familial identity of our family páńd́á [a Brahmin priest acting as a guide to pilgrims at holy places] was Shlaogram Bhandarii Panda – “Four and a half brothers”. I was very young at the time. I asked Bhandarii Páńd́á or the eldest brother, “Well, how is it you are four and a half brothers? I can clearly see that you are five.”

Páńd́ájii answered, with a beaming smile, “ Just see here, my child, I am one; my next brother is one; my third brother is one; my fourth brother is one and my fifth brother is half, so it comes to four and a half.”
I asked Páńd́ájii, “Why do you count your youngest brother as a half? He is in fact taller than you.”
Páńd́ájii again beamed, “We four are married, and so each is one. The youngest one is still unmarried, and so he is only half!”
Well, of the four brothers, all were foolish sons [santán ( 1 ) in Bengali] of an educated father.

The eldest brother was a fool, a real idiot. The second brother was also like that and the third was no better. But the youngest one, although illiterate, no doubt, was quite intelligent. Moreover, he was also a jester. The four brothers were spending their days in great economic hardship. Then, suddenly, they heard the news that the king of a certain country had announced that he would amply reward anyone who who could compose and then recite the poem before him. But writing a poem is no joke. Someone may have an idea but no language to express it, while others have the command of language but no ideas to express, then there are yet others who have neither. Only someone who has both is a poet. Otherwise, one would write poems like the following:
Pátáy pátáy paŕe nishir shishir,
Táte kii vá áse yáy bhoṋdár pisiir.
[The nocturnal dews fall on leaves, but what does it matter to the sister of Bhondaʼs father?]
When the king saw that no poet capable of writing a rhymed couplet reported to the royal court, he conceded that even a one line poem would do. For example,
Kii ye likhi chái máthá o muńd́u ám-i kii bujhi tár kichu.
[Do even I understand the meaning of the rubbish that I compose?]
The problem was now solved for the four brothers. They felt like malaria patients in remission after heavy sweating.
The eldest brother said, “I can do it!” [I can write a one-line poem.]
The second brother said, “I also can write one.”
The third brother said, “I can also write a verse.”
The youngest brother said, “I can also write poems in rhymed verse.”

They decided that at seven the next morning they would start out for the royal court, [so that they would arrive] at the most auspicious hour to read poems to the king. In the small hours of the morning the eldest brother went to the field with a gáŕu [ a pitcher or tankard with a spout, usually with a handle] in his hand, to get into a poetic mood. A gentle breeze was blowing, a poetic mood started coming to him, and the dark spots on the moon made it look like a slightly burnt chapati that had been overcooked. Then he suddenly noticed that there were three holes in front him, and there was water in all three holes, reflecting a moon in each, and there was one more in the sky. So, there were altogether four moons on earth. The eldest brother felt sudden poetic inspiration and wrote a line, Candra cáru [Four moons]. The eldest brother returned home hastily with the gáŕu [water pot] in hand and told his brothers, “Iʼve got it! Eureka, eureka! Now a fine one-line verse is on my lips.”

Without wasting a moment, and also taking a gáŕu, the second brother ran in the same direction and sat under a bak tree [Sesbania grandiflora] but he couldnʼt get into a poetic mood. Meanwhile, the moon had set, causing a real problem in setting the mood. Around that time, a bak flower fell on his head and immediately he was electrified by poetic inspiration, instantaneously composing a one-line poem: Mátháy phul paŕe – bakadháru [Flower drops on the head, the holder of bak flower].
With hectic speed he returned with the gáŕu because after some time they were to start for the royal court.

The third brother could not afford to delay. By the time he went to the field and sat down, the sun had already risen. In the sunshine, the copper gáŕu not only glittered but also became hot. The third brother was at once struck by poetic inspiration and composed a one line poem: Suryer uttápe támra gáŕu [The gáŕu made of copper is heated by the sun].
He ran back home, with the gáŕu in his hand, in such haste that he forgot to dip the gáŕu in the pond. After all, he was to start for the royal court shortly!
The three brothers, after dressing meticulously, set off (raváná ( 2 )) in Bengali].
The youngest brother also joined them. The elder brother asked, “Why are you coming with us? Are you a poet like us?”
He said, “While going such a long distance with you I shall also be touched by a poetic mood. At the royal court I shall also have a go at poetry.”
After some time all the four brothers reached the royal court, and they were called one by one. The eldest brother read out his one line poem, Candra cáru.
The king called his treasurer and told him, “Give him twenty-five rupees as a reward.”
The second brother went in and recited – Mátháy phul paŕe – bakadháru.
The king told the cashier, “Give him twenty-five rupees as his fee.”
The third brother then appeared and read out the one-line poem, Suryer uttápe támra gáŕu.
The king told the cashier, “Give him twenty-five rupees as his parting fee.”
Then the youngest brother came and told the king, “Oh honourable king, I shall read out a poetic verse to you.”
The king said, “Very well, very well, please go ahead.”

He first pointed out his three brothers and then pointed the finger towards himself and said: “Ei je ámrá cárti bhái – goru” [We four brothers here are cows. This is a play of words – goru (cows), rhymes with the last word in each of the other three brothersʼ attempts, while making a joke about their low standard of poetry.]
The king was very pleased and told his treasurer, “Give him fifty rupees toward salutation fees.”
The story does not end here. The king then appointed the youngest brother as a jester in the royal court.

There was once an Englishman with a bright red complexion and an unforgettable name. His full name was possibly Mr. Butterbread Laughingstock. That Englishman once travelled the whole world in search of a famous talker. He went around the world for the second time in search of a famous jester. On his first trip, the people of Bengal encouraged him. Thinking that the Bengalis would encourage him the second time as well, he went to Kolkata. The first time, when he went to China and met the most famous talker of that place, he came to know, on enquiry, that his name was Mr. Gu Ling. From there he flew to London ( 1 )Heathrow airport on a non-stop flight. After speaking to many eminent talkers of England, he came in contact with Sardar Bacan Bagiish [the greatest talker]. On asking his name, he came to know that his name was Mr. Gulist [the word gul, a slang in Bengali, means “a lie”]. From there he went to Paris ( 2 ), the capital of France. There, after making acquaintance with the famous talkers of the place he came in contact with the highest award-winning talker, whose name was Monsieur Gulon. From there he went to Berlin ( 3 ). On being introduced to the greatest talker of the place, who was also a noted film star he came to know that his name was Herr Guler. From there he went to Roma ( 4 ), the capital of Italy ( 5 ). On reaching there he enquired about their greatest talker and it did not take much time to find him. On enquiry he learned that his name was Signor Gulini. Next he went to Moscova ( 6 ).

The greatest talker of the place came to the airport in person, to welcome Mr. Butterbread Laughingstock. The name of the gentleman was Mr. Gulovaski. Then he flew to Mumbai on a direct flight and made an enquiry at a famous studio there. On enquiry, he found that the great actor who had became famous for his loquacity was named Gulkumar. Next, he went to Dehli. There in Chandni Chowk he came in contact with the greatest fibbing expert, and on enquiry, came to know that his name was Shriiman Gulgul Prasad. Next he came to Kolkata. On arriving at Kolkata he saw that here were fibbing experts galore. In the streets and restaurants they were available in plenty. They were not prepared to recognize him as a fibbing expert. They told this Englishman, “Come and stay here as an apprentice in acquiring the art of fibbing. During the period of apprenticeship you will be temporarily named Udaygulu Vidyarthii [a neophyte of fibbing]”.

At this time Mr. Butterbread came in search of a jester. On his arrival there he had heard that on the southern railway line, in Camripota ( 7 ), there lived a jester named Cakitocakar Cakkotti. Mr Butterbread, alias (oraphe: The original Persian word is urph. It is pronounced as orophe in Bengali by mistake) Udaygulu Vidyárthii, went to the bank of a pond in search of him. At that time, Cakitacakor was selling fish that he had caught in the pond, to an agent from the town. The agent said, “Oh son of of Cakkotti, all the fish that you have are puṋt́i and khayrá, that is, small fry. I canʼt pay you a good price for these.”

Cakitocakor said, “You have only dealt in selling fish but you have never done any research on them. Had you done so, you would have realized that there is not a single khayrá, kharsolá or cunopuṋt́i in this pond. I arranged a meeting with the well-known traditional fishermen on the bank of this pond. They all gave the unanimous verdict that the fish of this pond, which are thought to be puṋt́i fish, are actually the offspring of rui fish [a kind of very delicious freshwater fish, Labio rohita]. And the fish thought to be khayrá are actually the offspring of ilish [hilsa fish]. Here, the great sage Durbasa once expressed his desire to have a dish of rui fish with mustard seed paste and a hot broth of hilsa fish. The sage, sitting on a kush-mat and having performed the necessary ritual before lunch, anxiously waited [in Bengali this is called ha-pityesh ( 8 )] for the food. Impatiently, he started counting time but the hot fish broth never arrived. The villagers said, “We donʼt want to be drowned in an ocean of sin by feeding fish to the sage”.

The sage flew into a rage. He started moving very fast towards the abode of the gods, with his wooden sandals clacking all the way, to find out whether hot fish broth with mustard seed paste was available there. Before leaving, he angrily tore off his sacred thread and gave a curse: “May the rui and hilsa fish of this pond never grow in size!” Since then, the fishes have not grown large, but their quality is intact. And when their quality is intact, why should you not pay the proper price?
Just then, Mr. Butterbread arrived at the spot.

It is said that “Like attracts like ( 9 )”. After a short chat, Cakito Cakkotti and Butterbread Laughingstock became friends, and soon they became quite chummy and cemented their friendship. Mr. Butterbread took Cakito Cakkotti with him to Bilet ( 10 ) [the UK]. There, they spent their time quite happily for a few days. One day, Mr. Butterbread pointed out to Cakito Cakkotti a castle situated on the top of a high hill, and said, “Cakkotti, the castle that you see over there is the place where I was born, thirty-five years ago.” Cakito Cakkotti appreciatively said, “Ah! You were born in a lovely place, indeed.” After some time, Mr. Butterbread asked Mr. Cakito Cakkotti “Brother, where were you born, incidentally?”
Cakito Cakkotti said, “I was born in a hospital.”

Mr. Butterbread was so astonished, that with eyes almost as big as size 5 footballs, he wondered aloud – “How come? How come, in a hospital? What was the disease that attacked you at such a young age?”

While Mr. Butterbread and Mr. Cakito Cakkotti were busy chatting on a park bench, a huge, hefty fellow with a full beard walked up to Mr. Butterbread and said, “Hello, Butterbread, hello, Laughingstock, how are you? Do you recognize me?”
Butterbread looked at him and said, “Sorry, I canʼt really place you. I canʼt recognize you.”

The stranger said, “How can you say that? We once studied at the same school, in the same class, sitting side by side on the same bench. But today you canʼt recognize me? How strange, how really strange!”
Butterbread said quietly but very firmly, “No, I donʼt recognize you from my school, or from the bench where I used to sit. There was never such a huge, hefty fellow with a beard sitting next to me.”
One day, Mr. Butterbread told Cakito Cakkotti, “Do you know, Cakkoti, in my life I have survived two mighty storms. One was the gentle breeze of comedy and the other was the cyclone of tragedy.”

Cakito Cakkotti said, “Tell me, tell me about it. I would very much love to hear it. Ah, I feel pity for your tragedy even before I have heard about it, and for your comedy I feel like congratulating you. Anyway please let it out, let me listen to you.”

Butterbread said, “Do you know, what rarely happens on the earth has happened in my life. My birthday and my wifeʼs birthday are on the same day. That means, by elaborately celebrating one birthday we celebrate both. And there are two parts of the tragedy. One part is that since we have a common birthday we get fewer gifts than we would have got had there been two separate birthdays. Do you understand? Isnʼt it a tragedy! (Mr. Butterbread gulped thrice). And the large second part of the tragedy is that we cannot celebrate our birthdays every year.
Cakito Cakkotti asked, “Why? How can that be? How inauspicious!”
Mr. Butterbread said, “Our birthday falls on 29 February, so our birthday appears only every four years. Isnʼt it sad!”

Cakita Cakkotti sympathized, “Really, itʼs unfortunate that such a great tragedy could happen in a personʼs life. On thinking about your sorrow, my friend, I feel like jumping into the Thames and committing harakiri ( 11 ).”
Now it was Cakito Cakkottiʼs turn to speak. He said, “My life is full of tragedy and the tragedy started from the inauspicious moment when I got married.”
Mr Butterbread said, “Why? How is that? How sad, how bad it is, really!”

Cakito Cakkotti said, “Never a day passes when my wife doesnʼt quarrel with me and threaten, 'Now I am going to my parents, letʼs see who serves you food.ʼ And you know, Mr. Laughingstock, another tragedy is – a tragedy that has never befallen any human fate – (Cakito Cakkotti gulped seven times, counting them one by one, and then said,) and that is ... and that is ... and that is my wedding day and my wifeʼs wedding day are on the same day!”
Butterbread said, “Strange, really strange! Itʼs a miracle, really a miracle! My friend, where can you keep such sorrow? Youʼd better give a portion of your sorrow to me.”

Cakito Cakkotti returned to Camripota after his trip to Britain. He used to work at a railway office in Sealdah and commute from Camripota daily. Every day he was late in reaching his office. He used to reach by the last local train. One day he decided, “Tomorrow I shall make an historic exception, I must go to Sealdah by the first local train. If I canʼt go I shall change my name to Sacakita ( 12 ) Cakkotti.” The next morning, on waking up, Cakito Cakkotti looked at his wrist watch and saw that it was 7.35. He would have to finish everything quickly, and he thought, “Itʼs only twenty-five to eight, so there is enough time in hand. Let me have my morning tea in bed. Today I must do everything by the clock.” He again looked at his watch, “Twenty-five to eight. Thereʼs enough time. Let me read the newspaper. Today I wonʼt budge an inch from the hands of the clock. Let me see what the time is. Oh, itʼs just seven thirty-five. Thereʼs enough time. On this winter day, let me thoroughly massage some mustard oil on my body and bask in the sun. Today, I should be called Gharimáná Cakkotti [Cakkotti, the absolutely punctual one] instead of Cakito Cakkotti. Oh, I am surprised to see how steadily I am keeping a watch on the clock. Let me see, what time is it?
Oh, itʼs seven thirty-five. Thereʼs enough time. Let me go and have a swim and bathe in the pond. On other days I have no time for swimming.”

After taking his bath, Cakito Cakkotti sat down to have his lunch. He looked at his watch, “35 minutes past seven, enough time.” He told the women folk of the house, “Every day I rush for the train after somehow gulping down my food, without any time to chew the dáṋt́á caccaŕi [a preparation made from the stems of vegetables]. Today I have enough time, so give me a generous portion of sajne dáṋt́á [the long, edible seedpods of the drumstick tree]. Let me enjoy chewing them to my heartʼs content.”
Finally, Cakito Cakkotti finished his lunch. He thought that he had better catch the first local train and not delay any longer.

When Cakito Cakkotti reached Camripata station, chewing betel leaves all the way, Chidam Mudi, who sold betel leaves and biri from his four-legged shack, said, “Hello, son of Cakkotti, why are you going to the station so late in the day?”
Cakito Cakkotti asked, “What do you mean by 'late in the dayʼ? I have come to the station to catch the first local train.”
Chidam Mudi said, “Are you insane? Even the last local left an hour ago!”

Cakito Cakkotti said, “Thatʼs not possible. Thatʼs simply impossible. That canʼt have happened. Impossible! Impossible! The driver and the guard must have started the train at the wrong time. I havenʼt made a mistake. I couldnʼt have made a mistake. A human can make a mistake once or twice or thrice, but I checked the time seventeen times and I ensured that it was seven thirty-five. The world can make mistakes but Cakito Cakkotti can never go wrong”.

We get two words, daḿshana and dashana by adding the suffix anat́ to the verbal root daḿsha. The word daḿshana means “to bite”. Dashana means “tooth” because people bite with their teeth. You can use the words danta, data or dashana, because each of them means dáṋt [tooth]. A person whose teeth are as white as jasmine may be described as kundadanta, kundadashana or kundadata. For the feminine gender one can use kundadantii or kundadashaná. However, the word kundadatii is most in use.

In my childhood we used to hear a ghost story of two female ghosts who were always vigorously quarrelling with each other. They used to fight all the time. They were actually nanad-bháj [nanad: husbandʼs sister; bhaj: brotherʼs wife],that is, sisters-in-law. One was called Mrs. Kulokarnii ( 1 ), because her ears were as big as a kulo [a bamboo winnowing tray], and the other was called Mrs. Muladantii (grammatically, muladatii would have been more appropriate), because her teeth were as big as radishes. One was holding a handbag made of scorpion skin, while the other had a handbag made of the bones of large black ants. When these two ladies used to quarrel, while grasping their handbags and looking at the sky all the while, it was such a wonderful sight that it simply defies any description.

A photographer from Phurphura once told me that he had tried religiously as many as one thousand, one hundred and eleven times, counting each attempt on his fingers, to capture the scene with his technicolour video camera. But every time, he had returned disappointedly from Baratajpur, because both the female ghosts had chased him away with a stubby broom. Mrs. Kulokarniiʼs husband, Mr. Pindigela Bhut (P.G.B. for short) used to roam about in the fields and forests, among shrubs, bushes, bamboo groves and shyáoŕá trees, in order to escape the cacophony of those quarrels. When the other ghosts asked him, “Hayaṋ gáṋ tumi saṋv saṋmay baṋŕiir báṋire báṋire kenaṋ tháṋka gáṋ?” ( 2 ) [Hello, why do you always stay away from your house?] He would reply, “Áṋmáṋr haṋrt́er baṋyámoṋ áṋche kinṋaṋ, táṋi dáṋktár baṋleṋecheṋ khoṋlá háṋoyáy tháṋkteṋ.” [Since I have cardiac trouble, the doctor has advised me to remain in the open air].

For the last five hundred years these female ghosts have been contesting for the post of the Minister of the Department of Womenʼs Welfare of the State of Bhagariistan [a wasteland for depositing the dead bodies of animals], but they have not been able to win even once. The post was won by ordinary women, instead.

When somebody wears an affected smile conspicuously revealing their teeth, while suppressing their actual feelings, it is called dáshanikatá ( 1 ) in Sanskrit. While etymologically the word da , formed by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root dam is dáshanikatá, meaning “the smile of a person baring their teeth, while suppressing their actual feelings”, the word, in a general sense, indicates a situation where one supports somebody in public without actually supporting them in oneʼs heart. If somebody, while actually happy, sheds crocodile tears, that is also called dáshanikatá. This dáshanikatá is only another name for deceptive behaviour. Many of you have personal experience of dáshanikatá. I also have such experience. Let me tell you about one or two such small incidents in this connection.

For any human to pretend not to desire a certain thing, while actually hankering after it, is certainly a kind of dáshanikatá. As the story goes, Ravana kept Sita as a captive in an ashoka forest [a grove of flame trees] and Sita was guarded by a host of ceŕii ( 2 ) [female guards].

Sita was crying loudly, remembering Rama. Ravana had told the female guards, “Keep a watch on Sita and see that she cannot repeat the name of Rama. In case she calls his name, torture her. The female guards were, in fact, devotees of Sita-Ram [Sita and Rama]. They saw that here was an opportunity to say “Sita-Ram”, so they started addressing Sita, “Sita, donʼt say Ramaʼs name. Sita, donʼt say ‘Rama’. Sita, donʼt call out Ramaʼs name.” As a result, the female guards got an opportunity to say “Sita-Ram”.

In North India most people are Vaeśńavas [worshippers of Viśńu], while a few are Shaevas [worshippers of Lord Shiva]. There are hardly any worshippers of Shakti [the goddess Káli], the Sun or Gańapati [lord Ganesh]. Among the Vaeśńavas, the devotees of Sita-Ram outnumber the devotees of Radhe-Shyam [Radha and Krśńa]. Since there are more votaries of Sita-Ram than of Radhe-Shyam, one gets more opportunity to hear the word Sita-Ram than Radhe-Shyam in the streets. Those who want to hear Radhe-Shyam therefore have recourse to a ruse. If, on seeing them, the small boys of the locality say “Sita-Ram, Sita-Ram”, they say, “Sánanda raho bet́á, sánanda raho” [Be happy, my child, be happy]. And if the small boys, on seeing them, say “Radhe-Shyam, Radhe-Shyam” they pretend to be angry and chase them away. The small boys retrace a few steps in fear and then again start taunting, “Radhe-Shyam”. In this clever way, the person gets the opportunity to hear their favourite name, “Radhe-Shyam”.

In my childhood, [a gentleman named] Saukhilal, who lived in our neighbourhood, used to become angry on hearing the word “Radhe-shyam”, and used to bless us on hearing “Sita-Ram”. So, being children, we used to shout “Radhe-Shyam, Radhe-Shyam” whenever we saw him, and he would chase us angrily.

I was about five at the time. One day, I decided not to run away in fear. Let me stay and see what Saukhilal wants to say, I thought. When we saw Saukhilal, my friends and I all shouted “Radhe-Shyam, Radhe-Shyam”, and Saukhilal ran after us. Everyone fled except me. Saukhilal picked me up in his arms and took me to his house. There, he treated me to a bellyful of kesariyá peŕá ( 3 ) and khájá [delicious Indian sweets]. Then he said, “Haṋ haṋ bábuá ( 4 ) rádhe-shyám, rádhe-shyám, rádhe-shyám, khub boli heṋ. Hameshá shuneyar (ra must be fully pronounced) hámárá man cáhaeche”. [Yes, my dear child, please keep on saying “Radhe-Shyam, Radhe-Shyam, Radhe-Shyam”. My mind yearns to hear it all the time].

I had a close friend whose name was Kali Kinkar Kahali, from Majdia in Nadia District (madhyadviipa >majjhadiiya > májdiá). In ancient Bengal, a village surrounded by a river, canal or marsh was called diyá or dihá). Majdia was then part of the Krishnaganj police station area, of the district subdivision of Chuadanga of the then undivided ( 5 ) Bengal.

Kalikinkarʼs father, Mukundalal Kahali, was an eminent homeopath. Kalikinkarʼs mother was a great devotee of Krśńa, and, on looking at Kalikinkar, one would think that he was a devotee of the goddess Káli. It was impossible to elicit from him the name of Krśńa or any word related to Krśńa, even by mistake, and in these matters his presence of mind was very sharp. Once, I thought that whatever Kalikinkar might do, he would not be able to distort a historical truth or a universal truth. With an intention to trap him, I told him, “Well, Kalikinkar, my knowledge of geography is very poor. Can you tell me under which police station your Majdia comes?” He at once replied, “Káliganj ... Káliganj ... Káliganj”.

I said, “But Káliaganj is quite far from Majdia. Káliganj police station is on the eastern bank of the river Bhagirathi, near the town of Katwa in Burdwan district. How can the village Majdia come under its jurisdiction?”

The pat reply came: “Ours is Káliganj number one, and that is Káliganj number two.” I said, “Well, Nadia has been there since the time of the Pathans. I hear that once upon a time Nadia was under the jurisdiction of Chakla Jessore. Kasba is supposed to have been the district headquarters of Chakla Jessore. Later, Chakla Jessore split into two. One part continued as Chakla Jessore, and the other part was named Chakla Nadia ( 6 ). I hear that this Chakla Nadia was spread over a huge area, from Plassey in the north to the Bay of Bengal in the south; from the Bhagirathi in the west, to the Padma in the north-east, and to Jessore Chakla in the east. The district headquarters continues to be situated where it was in those days. I have been trying to remember the name of this town for quite a few days, but I am not able to recall it. Can you tell me the name of the district town of Nadia?” I started scratching my head when he said, “Canʼt you even recall this simple matter? It is Kálinagar... Kálinagar... Kálinagar!” [Actual name being Krishnanagar which Kalikinkar can never utter.]

I thought, let me catch out Kalikinkar in another way. I said, “Kalikinkar, you must have heard that Hooghly is a district with a rich cultural heritage. It is well-nigh impossible to find the likes of it in terms of temple sculptures and fine aesthetic taste. Bankura-Manbhum (Purulia-Dhanbad-Singbhum of the present time) has the greatest number of ancient temples. Mallabhum (the Bishnupur subdivision of Bankura district) has the greatest number of temples. But it is difficult to find a match for the temples of Hooghly District in matters of delicate artistry and fine sensibility. Let alone the temple of Anantavásudeva, Haḿseshvari of Banshbere and the Gupta Brindában temple of Guptipara, both the oldest church and the oldest mosque of Bengal are also situated in Hooghly district. The Imambara of Hooghly has a cultural heritage and the fame of Phurphurashariiph has spread far and wide.

The oldest college of Bengal is also in Hooghly, and the same is true about its press. The typefaces of the Bengali alphabet was first forged by Panchanan Karmakar, a great son of this district. And who does not know about the chariots of Chandannagar and Guptipara? The chariot festival of Mahesh–Ballabhpur is a living legend. Moreover, there are so many beautiful fairs with different attractions in this district! There was a time when merchants from abroad came to participate in the Khunti Fair of Hooghly. The fame of the Gosaighata Fair crossed the Indian border and reached foreign lands.

This is that Hooghly District! In the British period, a large proportion of Indian ICS officers came from this district alone. In the British period, when most of the districts in Bengal did not have a single college, Hooghly District had as many as four degree colleges. This is not a matter of any small pride. Mrs Chandramukhi Basu, the first woman M.A. of India, hailed from this district.

Is that all, Kalikinkar? You know that after eating a dull, monotonous vegetable dish of shákcaccaŕi [a cooked, dry dish of greens] continuously for days together, one likes to have a change, to have some tasty dishes, and for that Hooghly offers excellent scope. Has anybody ever seen or heard of such delicious, mouth-watering delicacies? How fine is the artistry of the confectioners of this place! It is said that in ancient times the gods used to come to Hooghly District in human form, just to eat sweets. This is that Hooghly District! This district was part of Burdwan District until the Moghul period.”

I said, “Well, Kalikinkar, if I remember correctly, your maternal auntʼs house is in this district, isnʼt it? These days, doesnʼt your cousin [maternal sisterʼs son], Professor Sannyal live in his ancestral home? Well, at which station do you get down in order to go to your auntʼs home?”
He said, “Donʼt you know that my aunt lives in Chatra?”
I said, “But there is no station at Chatra; where do you get down?”
He said, “You can get down at Seoraphuli.”
I asked him, “Is Seoraphuli the nearest station?”
He said, “No, the nearest station is Srikálipur” [in fact the nearest station is Shrirampur, but Kalikinkar would not take the name of Rama].
I said, “Well, your cousin is an eminent professor. He has been doing research on the villages of Janai and Manad for a long time. I would like to meet him briefly. Could you tell me his name?”

The name of Kalikinkarʼs cousin was Krishnakishore Sannyal, but Kalikinkar said, “The name of my cousin is Báṋkáthákur Syándel... Báṋkáthákur Syándel... Báṋkáthákur Syándel [ Not only did he not take the name of Krśńa, he made a distorted pronunciation of the actual title Sanyal out of sheer disdain]”.
I realized that however hard I tried, he would stick to his guns. Tel dáo siṋdur dáo bhavii bholbár nay [No amount of oil and vermilion can make a stubborn person give up their pursuit].

The other day I was returning home after a morning walk. There were practically no people in the marketplace. Suddenly, I noticed that Kalikinkar was returning home, carrying a huge cluster of káṋt́álii kalá ( 7 ) that he had just bought.
It dawned on me that Kalikinkarʼs mother, a great devotee of Viśńu, worshipped Satyanáráyańa every Sunday.
I asked him, “To which divine demesne are you going to so early, at dawn, with a cluster of káṋt́álii kalá?”
He said, “My mother worships Satyakálii every Sunday, thatʼs why.” [Náráyańa is another name of Viśńu.]

Once, Helárám Cát́ujje [Chatterjee], the famous Rámáyańa singer, came with his troupe from Bankura to our town for a Rámáyańa recital. All the people of the place were charmed by his presentation and rendition.

Immediately, a powerful committee was formed in the locality. The two local leaders – Rádhikáranjan Roy and Rádháraman Datta – took the initiative so that the Rámáyańa recital of Helaram could be continued there for quite some time. Kalikinkar was an expert in collecting subscriptions, so the responsibility of collecting subscriptions for this naturally fell to him. One day, on seeing Kalikinkar moving from house to house with the subscription book, I asked him, “What are you collecting the subscriptions for?”
“There is a committee, and I am collecting the subscription at the request of the committee,” he replied.
“Who are the members of the committee, and what is the committee for?” I said.
“Kálikáranjan Ray and Káli Raman Datta are in the committee,” he explained.
“Please tell me what the committee is for?” I asked.

He said, “Helákáli Cátujje has come from Bankura. He is giving a first-class rendition of the Kali-áyan [Kalikinkar used the word Kali-áyan in place of Rámáyańa, because he would not utter the word Ráma]. I am just collecting subscriptions for that.”

I realized that it was impossible to catch Kalikinkar in a small net; so this time I cast my net very wide. I said, “You are intimately known to the Ráŕh region. You certainly know that the northern part of this very old Ráŕh region was known as Bardhaman bhukti [‘bhukti’ means ‘district’] and the southern part was known as Dandabhukti.”

Dandabhukti has not received as much recognition in history as Bardhaman bhukti has, for various reasons. For some unknown reason, historians did not pay any great attention to Dandabhukti. If somebody wants to write the history of Dandabhukti they will see that there is so much material that if properly organized, one can write several Mahábháratas. As many famous people were born in this region, similarly there are also innumerable towns and villages of great cultural heritage here. Towards the end of the Pathan period Dandabhukti was renamed Hijli, and towards the end of the Moghul period its name was changed to Madinápur. When the British got the civil rights of Bardhaman, 24 Parganas and Chattagram, along with Madinápur, they renamed it Midnapore. In the course of time its Bengali name became Medinipur. The district, which is very large, has also made such a significant contribution to the art of town planning and civilization, not only to the entire Ráŕh region but also to the entire civilized world that it is a veritable seat of human civilization. The sea that skirts it and the range of hills that border the district, sloping from north-west to the south-east, led to a magnificent opulence of all kinds of earthly treasures. Starting with Kalidas, the great poet, many great people were born in this district. In the Buddhist period, Dantapurivihár of this district, the present name of which is Dáṋton, was built upon the place where a receptacle containing the relics of the Buddhaʼs teeth – lay buried. It is here that Sarashaḿka, the most beautiful water tank, not only of the Ráŕh region but also of the entire Bengal, is situated.

Kanthi (Kanthiká), Tamluk (Támralipta), Chandrakona, Cheriaberia, Mahisadal, Kśirpai and Kheput́ are famous historical places, among many others.
