The district was in the forefront of the struggle for independence. Well, I forgot to name Neradeul, a very famous place of the district. I also forgot to mention Bogri-Krisnanagar. In Bengal there are a number of places named Krishnanagar.

Of these, three Krishnanagars became famous: (1) Goarii-Krishnanagar, the headquarters of Nadia district; (2) Khanakul-Krishnanagar of Arambag subdivision of Hooghly District; and (3) Bogri-Krishnanagar of Midnapore District.
I asked Kalikinkar, “Well, Kalikinkar, your father was an eminent physician, and I have heard that he used to practice in Krishnanagar. Which Krishnanagar was that?”
Without wasting any time Kalikinkar said, “All along my father practiced in Kanthi-Kálinagar.”
I realized that he was a deep water fish; he couldnʼt be caught even in a very wide net.

It was impossible to tackle Kalikinkar. I thought, let me make use of a sentiment. One does not really dilly-dally with oneʼs fatherʼs name. The name of Kalikinkarʼs father was Dr. Mukundalal Kahalii.
I said, “Kalikinkar, your father was an eminent physician, wasnʼt he?”

Kalikinkar said, “Does that need saying? Nobody had ever seen or heard of such a great homoeopath. A dose of Cina 200 administered by him could flush out one thousand worms from the body in one hour.”

I said, “When we refer to a doctor we either use his name or his title. For example, while referring to Dr Arun Báŕujje [Banerjee] of our place some used to refer him as Dr Arun and some as Dr. Banerjee. By which name was your father better known?”
He said, “He was better known as Dr. Kahalii.”
I asked, “How was his name written in the certificate?”
He said, “Ájebáje [meaning, nonsense, rubbish] Kahalii... Ájebáje Kahali... Ájebáje Kahalii.” [Mukundalal is another name of Viśńu.]
Kalikinkar at once left the place.

Many amusing stories are current about the irregularities of the Education Department. What was the origin of these stories? In addition to obvious indifference and indiscipline, there is also a conspicuous lack of ethics and prudence. While the statement that “no great work can be done by deception” is true, similarly it is equally true that when one passes an examination by a fluke, without working hard for it, there is neither proper acquisition of knowledge nor efficiency. Huge shortcomings persist.

In our locality lived Mr Pulakita Ray (Pulakita: he used to pronounce it pulkit), a Hindi teacher. In my childhood, teachers were addressed as mát́ár sáháb [Honʼble Sir] in Bihar. Pulakita Ray knew no English, and I have no idea of his proficiency in Hindi. He used to go the class wearing a dirty dhuti [loin cloth] raised above his knees, a phatuá [a kind of loose cotton waistcoat] full of betel leaf stains, and a gámchá [cotton napkin] on his shoulders. He used to carry a matchbox in one pocket and a bundle of biŕi in another pocket of the phatuá. He used to split each matchstick into two, lengthwise, so that he could get double the matchsticks originally in the matchbox. Immediately on reaching the school, the mát́ár sáháb used to take a bath at the adjacent tube well and then used to take chátu ( 1 ) [flour generally made of roasted chickpeas] (Sanskrit for cholár chátu is shaktu, and chátu made of barley or muŕi [parched rice] is called dhánáká or dhánácurńa in Sanskrit).

It did not take him much time to eat chátu with a mixture of oil, salt and chilli ( I also used to take chátu in the same way, not only because it was palatable, but also because, according to knowledgeable physicians, eating chátu that way gives a combined taste of bitter, sour, salty and sweet and activates the mind and the body. Eating chátu with milk and mango is also both tasty and invigorating.) At night he used to take rice at home. One day I saw that Mr Pulakita Ray was going to school with a full size dhuti and punjábii [a loose fitting upper garment with no collar] (In North India a punjábii is called Báḿlá kurtá [a Bengali shirt], with no betel leaf in his mouth and no matchbox in his pocket. I asked, “Kii holo che mát́ár sahib?” [“Whatʼs the matter today, sir?”]
Pulakita Ray said “Ái nispektar sáháb eyáitei” [Today the inspector will come to visit the school].

Many kinds of stories are current about the standard of education. Whether fact or fiction, they are basically realistic. There was an occasion when an inspector was about to visit the school. The teachers tried to clean up the school and keep everything trim and tidy. They also instructed their students to have a bath, brush their hair, and come to the school neat and clean, smartly dressed, with freshly washed clothes, and shoes.
A few students said, “Sir, we havenʼt got any shoes, what should we do?”
The teacher said, “Just borrow a pair from somebody and wear them only on that day.”
Another student said, “My maternal cousin has shoes, but his shoes are larger than my size.”
The teacher said, “It does not matter if the shoes are big. Just walk slowly, dragging your feet. But a smaller size will not do, because then you canʼt step into them.”

While talking about shoes, I remember an incident of my childhood days. One Budhuaʼs mother (named budhuá, because he was born on a Budhvár [Wednesday] used to work in our house. Budhua was admitted to a school. One day, on coming home from school, Budhua told his mother, “Má, tomorrow the inspector will visit the school. The teacher has asked me to go to school with shoes on.”

His mother bought a pair of shoes from the Raniganj market in Burdwan that very evening and gave it to him. The next day, Budhua took a bath after putting a lot of mustard oil on his head, carefully parted his hair, put on his new shoes and left for school. He was in such a hurry that he forgot to put on a shirt and trousers.

The teacher had told the students, “When the inspector comes to the class I will stand behind him. Whenever he asks you any questions I will tell you the answers through suggestions and gestures. Just keep watching me.”
The students said, “Yes sir, we will do that.”

The inspector first went to the Sanskrit class. The Sanskrit teacher had already decided not to sleep in the class that day. As soon as the inspector came in, he hastily stood up. As arranged, he stood behind the inspector The inspector asked a student, “Could you please tell me what is the plural form in the accusative of the word, go [cow]?”
Although the boy was intelligent, he did not know the answer. He looked askance at the Sanskrit teacher standing behind the inspector.

The plural in the accusative of the word go is gáh. In Bengali the body is called gá (gátra>gátta>gá-a>gá) . So the Sanskrit teacher started patting his own body from head to toe and vice versa, and thus he indicated his body [as the answer] to the student.

The student was over-intelligent. He was a cut above his teacher [If the teacher was molasses, he was sugar ( 2 )]. He thought, gá is a colloquial Bengali word, so it cannot be used in Sanskrit. The Sanskrit for gá is shariira. So he told the inspector, “Sir, the plural of go [cow] in the accusative is shariiram [body]”.

The inspector [nispektar] left the class in annoyance and disgust. He next went to the English class. As soon as he entered the class the English teacher stood behind him in order to give the necessary hints to the students. The inspector asked the students, “How do you pronounce the word F-U-T-U-R-E?” A very intelligent boy at once replied, “phut́ure, phut́ure”. The inspector felt disgusted but still asked, “Well, tell me what is the meaning of phut́ure”.

How could the English teacher give a hint that the word meant “things that are yet to happen”? He started showing the lines of his palm. By reading the palm one can know oneʼs future, so he showed the lines of the palm of his right hand. The boy who was questioned said, “Phut́ure means ‘right hand, the right hand of the English teacher’”.

Then the inspector asked another student, “Well, can you tell me the meaning of the word lotus?” The English teacher then pointed with his forefinger the pond behind the window at the back. There were many fully bloomed lotuses in the pond. He thought, “This time at least the result is certain. On seeing the lotuses the boy will be able to give the correct answer.”

The boy who was asked the question saw that the teacher was pointing towards the pond. Just at that moment, his paternal aunt [fatherʼs sister; pisimá, fatherʼs married sister] arrived at the pond to collect water in a pitcher.
The student said, “Lotus means... lotus means... lotus means... a paternal aunt holding a pitcher.”

The inspector not only felt annoyed and disgusted; he also felt somewhat anguished. He walked out of the class in extreme haste and entered the History [itihása ( 3 )] class.(In fact, what is taught in the class is not itihása but itikathá, which is called history in English and histoire in French).
The inspector asked the History teacher, “Are the cultural aspects of the Rámáyańa and the Mahábhárata part of the prescribed syllabus?”

The teacher said, “Yes sir, yes sir, yes sir, oh yes, yes, yes, yes, that goes without saying, that goes without saying. Our students not only remember them by heart, they are constantly on their lips as well, all the time.”
The teacher, as usual, took his position behind the inspector.
The inspector asked a student, “Tell me who broke the haradhanu [Shivaʼs bow – in an incident from the Rámáyańa]? Who broke the haradhanu?”
The first student implored almost tearfully, “I didnʼt break it, sir. I never indulge in any kind of breaking activities. I promise you, sir.”
The inspector then asked the second boy, “Can you tell me who broke the haradhanu?”

The second boy, while wiping the tears from his eyes with both hands, whimpered, “I didnʼt break it, sir. How could I have broken it, sir, since I have never seen a haradhanu with my own eyes? Had I broken it, sir, would the History teacher have spared me?”
The inspector felt very irritated and asked the third student, “Can you tell me who broke the haradhanu?”
Breaking down in tears, the boy said, “I didnʼt break it, sir. None of my friends broke it, sir. Possibly Kelo-Bhulo broke it, sir.”
The inspector asked, “Who is Kelo-Bhulo?”

The third student promptly replied, “They were my friends, sir. But the other day, when I had just taken a bite of a peyárá ( 4 ) [guava], they asked me to give it to them. I said, “Let me have another bite and then I will give it to you.” The boy started crying loudly and continued, “But they had no patience. They became cross with me. Possibly it is they who broke the haradhanu.” He resumed his wailing.
But the History teacher, standing behind the inspector all the time, waved his hand to suggest to the students that they should never admit that they had broken the haradhanu.

The inspector then looked at the History teacher and said, “What is this that I see? You said that they remember the Rámáyańa well; so much so that they can recite it any time, and yet they are not able to say who broke the haradhanu!”

The History teacher said, “Sir, if you give me your assurance, I can tell you that my students have told the truth. None of them broke the haradhanu. Moreover, how can I allow them to indulge in such perverse activities? And, to tell you the truth, sir, I did not break the haradhanu either. I have never seen it, in fact.”

The inspector, most displeased by now, entered the office of the Headmaster and told him, “Sir, how miserable is the educational standard of your school! I have been told that the plural of go in the accusative form is shariiram, that the pronunciation of the word ‘future’ is phut́ure, that ‘future’ means ‘the right hand of the English teacher’ and that ‘lotus’ means ‘a paternal aunt holding a pitcher’. What rubbish are you teaching in this school? And the matter of haradhanu surpassed all the rest. Instead of giving the right answer, all of them said, ‘I didnʼt break it, sir, I didnʼt break itʼ.”

The Headmaster said, “Sir, I am very sorry to see that you are displeased. I may not say anything about the educational standard of my school, but I would certainly claim that the moral standard of my school is very high. I can strongly affirm that no student of this school broke the haradhanu. Moreover, I can also assure you that neither I nor any of my teachers broke it. Let alone breaking it, we have never seen it, in fact. You are an educated person. Just think for yourself, how we can break something which we have never seen? Furthermore, why should we break it at all, for Godʼs sake? Had I come by it, I would have carefully sent it to the museum.”

The inspector left the school. On going back to his office the first thing that he did was to write a long letter to the Director of Public Instruction, apprising him of the entire situation. Though he anxiously awaited, there was no response to his letter. Time ticked on and on and on but no reply came.

After many reminders, the long-awaited reply suddenly came, after a long year had passed. The Director of Public Instruction wrote: “Dear Inspector, I have fully realized the substance of your letter. The standard of education in our country has really gone down very much. However, there is no point in creating trouble and making a fuss about the haradhanu incident. Once I know the exact price of it I shall issue an order to write off the amount. Please see that the office does not have to send any reminder in this regard.”

The use of ńa (naṋ), candrabindu [the nasal sign in the Bengali alphabet] is extremely limited, not only in the Bengali language but also in other areas. Since candrabindu is not much in use amongst the common people, it is used in the nasalized articulation of a ghost to differentiate between a human and a ghost. This is just the opposite of French. The French language is dominated by nasalization.

The other day I was talking to Bankachand Baṋŕujje [Banerjee ( 1 )] of Bansbere. He had once gone to Champdani to buy a fishing hook made of bell metal. On the way there he came to wide open space without any locality nearby. It was completely desolate. Evening was fast approaching and it gave him an eerie feeling. Then he came to Goruti (Gaurhát́i) forest. After he had gone a few steps he saw a huge mango tree, and noticed that Gauṋgá [the Ganges] was nearby. There were crocodiles in the river and tigers in the forest, so he climbed up to the topmost branches of the tree, still trembling in fear. The evening was quickly turning to night. Suddenly, he noticed that just a little below him, sitting on a thick branch, a woman was kneading some dough. The woman asked him, “Tumi keṋ gáṋ, eṋi ráṋt biṋrete maṋgd́áṋle uṋt́he baṋsecha háoyá khete, áṋámáder eṋkheṋe páṋrk-táṋrk neṋi baṋt́e kintu beṋrábár maṋta baṋŕa báṋŕa bháṋgáŕ toń áṋche, seṋkháne háṋoyá kheṋte geṋle, náṋ kena gáṋ? [Who are you that you have come for fresh air by climbing up to the topmost branches of the tree, at night? It is true that there is no park or places like that here, but there are many big wastelands for a stroll. Why didnʼt you go there for some fresh air?”
Bankachand said, “I did not go out for fresh air; I am going to Champdani.”
The woman said, “Have you then mistaken the mango tree for Champdani?”
Bankchand said, “No, itʼs not like that. I climbed up the tree in fear of a terrible tiger.”
The woman said, “Thatʼs fine, thatʼs really fine. Then you are my guest. Have you had your dinner? I can tell from your voice that you are thirsty.”
Bankachand saw that there was shining vermilion mark on the womanʼs forehead. So, instead of addressing her as “sister” he addressed her as boudi [elder brotherʼs wife].
He said, “ You are right boudi, I am thirsty.”
The woman stretched out her long arm, collected a pot of water from the Ganges flowing four miles away, and said, “Here you are, t́hákurpo [brother-in-law, husbandʼs brother], take this.”
By then Bankachand had forgotten his thirst. He wondered, “Who could this person be – a woman or a female ghost?”
Bankachand asked, “Who are you, boudi? Will you please disclose your identity?”

The woman answered, “Donʼt try to know my identity at the dead of night. It may create a problem for you, my dear t́hákurpo. In the morning, after sunrise, I shall disclose my identity and hide from you behind the tree.”
Bankachand started shivering. His whole frame began to shake and his heart started throbbing violently. He thought, “Oh God, where have I landed up?”
Bágher bhaye caŕlum gáche,
Bhut bale pelum káche.
[I climbed the tree in fear of a tiger and the ghost said “I have got you close to me”].]

The woman said, “Have a quick wash. I have not been able to cook much. I just have a few nucis [luci – a kind of small, thin saucer-shaped bread fried in ghee] and álurdam [a delicious dish made of potatoes cut into big pieces]. Do you know that the potatoes of Hooghly District are very famous? My fatherʼs line, my maternal line and my in-lawʼs line – all three belong to Hooghly district.”
After eating, Bankachanda felt more comfortable and less afraid. He said, “Baudi, I canʼt sleep, so please tell me a story.”

Baudi said, “My in-lawʼs are from the west, in Balarambati. My father is from Baidyabati, my maternal uncle is from Sibarambati, my fatherʼs sister is from Janai and my motherʼs sister is from Bhandarhati. I was married at the age of three. At the time of the marriage I was sucking the breast of my maternal grandmother. My husband was 87. He was an aristocratic Brahmin – kávya, vyákarańa, sáḿkhya, vedánta tiirtha, tarkacaiṋcu, tarkapaiṋmcánan [a great scholar of poetry, drama, the Vedas, philosophy, Vedanta and logic]. After our marriage, when the married women were blowing conch shells, my husband felt trepidation in his chest on account of the sound of the conch shells and died of cardiac arrest. While I was still lying on the lap of my grandmother, I became a widow.

Since I was a Brahminʼs daughter I could not be married twice. My grandmother slapped me on the cheek and said, “You miserable wretch [literally, ‘burnt-faced one’]! Why were you born into the house of a Brahmin? It is on account of this that you have to suffer so much. The elder brothers of my husband were ninety-two years old and above, and the younger brothers of my husband were then above sixty years old. They were talking amongst themselves, 'If we allow this one to survive she will enjoy the property; it doesnʼt matter whether she can buy or sell it. So it is better to burn this horrid girl along with her husband on the same funeral pyre, and make her a sati ( 2 ) [a widow who burns herself on her husbandʼs pyre]. Let this pitiable creature go to heaven and enjoy rice and fish ad infinitum. Scorched by the fire, I cried aloud and tried to jump off the pyre and run away. But the brothers of my husband fixed me to a bamboo cane and burnt me to death, having already tied up my hands and feet. They poured a lot of vermilion on the spot where they had burnt me and marked it as a secret place of sati and said, ”Ah! What a pious girl she was; she became a sati smilingly, at the age of three. Even now the girls of the village, before putting a vermilion mark on the forehead, touch the spot with a pinch of vermilion and pray, 'May I also become a sati like her.ʼ But do you know, t́hákurpo [husbandʼs younger brother]? These days, they [the widows] never become sati at the death of their husband. On the contrary, they take out the bunch of keys from their husbandʼs pocket and keep it in their own custody. Well, my t́hákurpo, in a weak, unguarded moment I talked my heart out to you. Since that time I have been living in this mango tree as a female ghost and I have decided to tell the tale of my sorrow to educated and cultured people whenever I come across them. And I shall request that the notorious scoundrels of society who have perpetrated inhuman barbarism in the name of the welfare of the society, and continue to do so, should be taken to task.”
While listening to the story of baudi, a female ghost, night gave way to dawn. Bankachand got down from the tree.

He said, “My baudi, who is a female ghost, can I know your name, please?” “Baudi”, the female ghost said, “I am your baudi, and that is my identity. I do not want to fan the scandal by telling my name.”
The female ghost asked Bankachand, “t́hákurpo, it will be very late by the time you return after buying the hook. Will you take some light refreshment with you?”
Bankachand said, “Last night I ate so much. I donʼt have any appetite so early, at dawn. Just tell me, how can I really eat anything now?”

The female ghost said, “In that case you just wait for a while. Let me prepare some refreshment and put it in a tiffin carrier so that you can take it along. Also take along a flask of milk. Take it when you feel thirsty. You know that the water of this place is not so hygienic”.

Bankachand said, “Baudi, just wait, let me touch your feet.” On trying to touch her feet, he could not find them. Moreover, he noticed that her heels were in the front. The female ghost said, “T́hákurpo, you have forgotten that I am a female ghost. Had I become a sati I could have gone to heaven, but I became a female ghost because I had an unnatural death. T́hákurpo, you are human, why should you try to touch the feet of a female ghost? Donʼt you know that the heels of ghosts are always in the front, and the toes are at the back?”
Táder sumukh dike guŕmuŕo ( 3 ) ár pechan dike pá.
[They have their heels in the front and the toes at the back].]

In order to touch the feet of the female ghost Bankachand then went behind her. But the female ghost made an earnest entreaty: “My t́hákurpo, you are an educated gentleman and I am just a female ghost living on a mango tree. Why should you touch my feet? Please, my t́hákurpo, please donʼt touch my feet to show your respect.”
But without paying any heed to her words, Bankachand went behind the female ghost, collected the dust of her feet and put it on his forehead and said,
“I feel that my touching your feet has made my birth on this earth meaningful. Please bless me so that I always remember your words.”
While telling me these things, Bankachand shed tears ceaselessly.

t: One day, I was wondering what could be the suitable Bengali for the phrase used above. While thinking about it, I was passing Belun, a village in Hooghly district. Evening had just fallen. Suddenly, I noticed that two tall women were shouting in nasal voices. One was holding an áṋshbaṋt́i [baṋt́i means a device specially for cutting fish and non-vegetarian stuff], and the other held a muŕojháṋt́á [a worn-out broom]. From their nasal tone I realized that they were not humans, but female ghosts. On listening to them I surmised that they were two sisters-in-law, [the wife of oneʼs husbandʼs brother].
chapterTitle: Even a Brinjal Plant Claims to Be a Tree

t: The younger sister-in-law was saying, “My husbandʼs monthly income is Rs. 3000, while your husbandʼs income is only Rs. 2000. Even so, I have to take my turn and suffer the heat of the kitchen hearth [using wood as fuel] for part of the day. But why should I suffer it? I will no longer run the kitchen. I would like to spend that time either going to the cinema or by enjoying fresh air by climbing a shyáoŕá tree [in traditional folk tales, ghosts like to live in these trees]. Your husband earns less, so you should do the cooking both times.”
chapterTitle: Even a Brinjal Plant Claims to Be a Tree

(I at once noted down these words in my notebook, realizing that this is the appropriate Bengali for erańd́oapi drumáyate.) You come from a very poor family. You had never seen Rs. 3000 at a time since your birth. On coming here you saw it and it went to your head. From today onwards, donʼt introduce yourself as a female ghost because that will only provoke peopleʼs laughter. Furthermore, it is not true that your husband really earns Rs. 3000 per month. His actual salary is just barely Rs. 1000, and the rest he manages by smuggling bed sheets, towels, medicines and phenyl from the hospital to the black market. Today I will burst the balloon of your Rs. 3000 lie. I shall inform the officers of the Intelligence Department about this pilfering and smuggling (‘Detective’ means ”intelligence“. The word t́ikt́iki [lizard] has come form the word ‘detective’). They will crack down on your scoundrel husband, rope him in and send him to jail.”

t: The inherent weaknesses which harm humans are called ripus [enemies]. And the kind of constraints that attack a human by taking opportunity of these ripus and oppress him like a millstone around his neck, are called pásha. The ripus are six in number: káma [desire], krodha [anger], lobha [avarice], mada [pride or vanity], moha [blind attachment], mátsarya [jealousy]; and the bonds which bind a person on account of the presence of these ripus are called páshas [pásha means bandhanarajju ( 1 ) or bondage]. They are eight in number:
Ghrńá-shauṋká-bhayaḿ-lajjá-jugupsá ceti paiṋcamii,
Kulaḿ-shiilaiṋca-mánaiṋca aśt́ao páshah prakiirttitah.

Thus, hatred, doubt, fear, shyness, censure, vanity of lineage, cultural superiority complex, and egotism are the eight bondages. The biijamantra [acoustic root] of the bondage of hatred is pa. A bond does not necessarily relate to only one ripu; it can involve several. However, the bondages of hatred and fear, in spite of their association with other ripus are mainly related to the ripu of attachment. Suppose somebody is addicted to drinking. The mind moves downward when the attraction is materialistic. The verb pat [patati] is used for the downward motion. The addiction leads to oneʼs fall. And when the motion is upward it is called anurakti and the ultimate form of anurakti is called bhakti [devotion]. This is the reason why the verb in Sanskrit for such movement is urdhva gam (urdhvagacchati). One who has the weakness of an addiction to drinking becomes easily bound by hatred and fear. Not only addiction to drinking, any kind of attachment makes one both detestable to others and afraid of others. One runs after a delusion without any rhyme or reason. This idea of attachment brings a story to my mind.

An acquaintance of mine lived in Mominpur – I canʼt exactly recollect his name, possibly it was Mańd́ámohon Mukhujje. Some people called Mandamohan an extremely niggardly miser, some said he was a myopic miser, some said he was so closefisted that even water would not pass through his fingers. Some said that if he had to spend even one pice, he would feel as if he had broken a rib; some said that he was “one pice father, mother” [for him, to part with even a single pice is like to give up his father or mother], some said he was “one pice pyáṋjphulurii [onion vegetable chop]”, some humourously called him pyáṋj-payjár. Modern boys called him “upurhasta no-not-never” [he who never extends his hand in a giving gesture, one who never gives anything]. He immensely enjoyed all these appellations.

That year there was an overproduction of brinjal. The farmers in a country where there is no scientific economic structure become practically ruined when there is an over production. That year, the farmers of Bengal were practically ruined on account of the over production of brinjal. Once, I went to the village of Bego under the Haringhata Police Station in Nadia District and there I saw that the farmers where cutting brinjal into pieces and, after adding some salt, giving them to the cows. As soon as a cow which was about to eat it noticed that it was brinjal, it turned its face away and said humbá humbá. As it tried to take its food from another part of the pot, it saw brinjal there also and again it refused to eat. The farmers realized that if the cows stopped eating fodder they would not yield any milk, so they stopped serving brinjal to the cows.

The farmers of Ramnagar of Birbhum District were traditional cultivators of brinjal. On going there I heard that they had stopped plucking the brinjal from the plants. They told me, “Sir, let the brinjal rot on the plants. It will be more useful as compost.” I could not go to Panjipara for lack of time, so I cannot say what happened to the famous brinjal of that place. In those days, articles were sold in the wholesale market in our town in pasurii. Five seers made one pasurii and eight pasuriis made one mund. But there was no uniform measure of seer in all the districts. A standard seer meant eighty tolás [1 tola is 11.664 grams, so a standard seer would be 933.12 grams]. But in our Monghyr District a seer was eighty four tolas. Again, in the neighbouring district of Bhagalpur, it varied from a hundred, a hundred and one, and a hundred and three tolás in different places. In some places, a seer was even a hundred and five tolás.

A seer made of sixty tolás was called káṋci account [rough calculation]. Anyway that year, on account of the over production of brinjal, brinjal was aplenty in our town. In Mańd́ámohanʼs house the regular menu for three months at a stretch was rice and burnt brinjal. The women of the locality used to ask Mońd́ámohanʼs wife, Shrimatii Mithyámayii Devii [mithyá means “lies”], “Well, mother of Markat (The name of Mańd́ámohanʼs son was Markat́mohan [markat́ means “monkey”] Mukhujje. He used to sell lottery tickets and do private tuition. He would have his tiffin in the homes of his students, but preferred to chew harimat́ar ( 2 ) on holidays, that is, he preferred not to eat anything) . She used to answer, “Today, from early dawn until twelve noon, I worked continuously in the kitchen, so I have aches in my neck and back.”

People asked her, “What did you spend such a long time cooking?” She said, “ First I prepared a dish of brinjal and margosa leaves; then I prepared a dry dish of brinjal stalks, then grilled brinjal, then brinjal balls, then brinjal broth with pasted ginger, a hot dish of brinjal with pasted mustard seed, and finally a sweet dish made of brinjal seeds with sugarcane molasses. I also wanted to prepare a dish of brinjal with paddy seeds, but that could not be done because the fire in the oven became low by then. I donʼt allow burnt brinjal anywhere near my kitchen (I never ever cook burnt brinjal. That is only for poor people).”
As is the god so is the goddess.

Come what may, let me come to the point. At that time in our town, brinjal was selling for one pice a pasurii, two ánnás for a mund or one pice for five seers. Mańd́ámohan [mańd́á means “a kind of sweet”] Mukhujje asked a kujrá ( 3 ) [vegetable vendor] to give him one pice worth of brinjal. The vendor gave him five seers of brinjal and also gave a few brinjal [eight or ten] free. Mańd́ámohan said, “The extra brinjal that you have given free are enough for me. I donʼt need to buy any brinjal. Refund my money.”
Needless to say, such people as Mańd́ámohon become hated by others. Such a person also fears others. Thus, Mońd́ámohan became the object of hatred for everyone.

Once, in our locality, preparations for Kali Puja [worship of the goddess Káli] were being made with great pomp and show. Some boys were busy with theatre rehearsals. Some of them felt an acute shortage of money. Earlier, they used to manage some money from the shopping expenses of the family, but now, on account of growing expenses, their father started doing the shopping, himself. To combat the resultant lack of commission, some of the overenthusiastic boys started going around collecting subscriptions. People paid subscriptions according to their capacity. When Mańd́ámahon was asked to pay a subscription, he was visibly shocked. He said, “Oh God, you are talking about Kali! She is a great, belligerent lady, and we are devout Vaeśńavas. We canʼt worship Kali, it is forbidden by our ancestors.”

The boys thought, “Maybe there is a restriction.” And so they left. The next day all the people of the locality were invited to sit in rows and eat the maháprasáda, the food that had been offered to the goddess Kali. It was noticed that the person who sat first in the front row was none other than Shri Mańd́ámohon Mukhujje.
His friends asked, “ Hello, Mańd́ámohon, how come you are here? You said you are not allowed to worship the goddess Kali.”

Mańd́ámohon said, “I said that I am not allowed to worship but I never said that I am not allowed to eat the maháprasáda of the mother goddess. Let alone the big animals like elephants and horses, even the small insects cannot survive for a day without the grace of the mother goddess. How do you and I survive? Only because of the grace of the mother goddess. So you tell me now what wrong I have done by sitting here to eat the food offered to the goddess.” It is something like this:
Ámi beháyá petechi pát,
Kon beháyá ná dey bhát.
[Shameless as I am, I have sat down for food; Let me see if anyone is shameless enough not to serve me food.]

A story which is historically famous comes to my mind. The name of the village was Kuŕiye Kháoyá [eating leftovers]. Mr. Kipt́ekaiṋjus Kar [Kipt́e means “an extremely miserly person”] was a famous man of that place. Kipt́ekaiṋjus used to earn a lot of money in various legal and illegal ways. It dawned on him that if he wanted to suddenly become rich, it would be necessary to get a boon from Lord Shiva. To please other gods, it is necessary to perform a long and difficult penance. But Shiva is Bholanath [one who easily forgets peopleʼs misdeeds] and Ashutośa [One who is easily satisfied]. He becomes happy even if one offers him one ákanda flower [Calotropis gigantea] and a few leaves of the bel [Aegle marmelos] tree. So he decided to worship him.

Kipt́ekaiṋjus knew that Shiva is an incarnation of compassion. The demons and rákśasas [one of the indigenous races of India, who were misnamed thus by the Aryans] used to get boons from him. Kipt́ekaiṋjus started performing penance for Shiva. After a few days, Shiva, satisfied with his penance, appeared before him and said, “Open your eyes, my son, I am here.”
Kipt́ekaiṋjus said, “As you have come, my Lord, please fulfill my wish.”
Shiva asked, “What is your wish? Do you want me, or you want something from me?”
Then Kipt́ekaiṋjus said, “You are just a beggar with your body smeared with ashes. What would I do with you? You would become a liability for me. You better give me a boon so that I can make money.
Shiva said, “Just now you said that I am a beggar with ashes on my body. Then how can you ask for money from me?”

Kipt́ekaiṋjus said, “That you are a beggar with ashes smeared on your body is an established fact. But in the afternoon, after lunch, Kuber, the god of wealth, comes to massage your body. When, during the course of massaging you, Kuber tells you, 'Lord, now please turn on your right side,ʼ you can take the opportunity to tell him, 'Kuber, please be kind to Kipt́ekaiṋjus. Get him somethingʼ”.
Lord Shiva said, “But if Kuber does not care to oblige me?”
Kipt́ekaiṋjus said, “Who is there in the three worlds who can refuse you? Kuber must listen to you.”
Shiva said, “Well, I shall tell Kuber, and I will let you know what he replies.”

Kipt́ekaiṋjus said, “Lord, it is after doing penance for quite a few days that I have been granted an interview with you. Another interview will mean penance for many more days. Meanwhile, the sales in my shop have almost reached bottom. So tell me in advance, on the basis of what you guess would be the reply of Kuber, what I should do.” Shiva thought, “What a pity! Why should the poor fellow do penance for me again and again? Alas, the poor fellow, the poor fellow bogged down in illusion!”
Shiva said to Kipt́ekaiṋjus, “Start walking straight through that vast forest [arańyánii ( 1 ) ] extending to the horizon. I shall inform Kuber about it and he will take the necessary action.”

Kipt́ekaiṋjus started moving on and on with interminable speed. He did not look at the trees because he had not come to do research on plants. He did not take note of the way the birds and animals lived because he had no time to think about them. Was he thinking of Lord Shiva? No, certainly not. Lord Shiva was now closed out of his mind. Was he thinking of Kuber? No, not him, either. He was thinking of Kuberʼs wealth.

Kipt́ekaiṋjus travelled on. He was not afraid of tigers, nor of snakes, nor of crocodiles emerging from the water. He was lost in thoughts of wealth; this strong attachment blurred his vision. He had no time to ponder what others would say or think. He walked on and on, through his extreme greed for money. Suddenly, something came into view and Kipt́ekaiṋjus stopped. He was not able to believe his eyes. In front of him there was a hill of cowries [kaŕi ( 2 )], on his right there was a mountain of cowries, on the left there was a hillock of cowries and at the back a mound of cowries. He declared victory. But whose victory? Not the victory of Shiva, nor the victory of Kuber. It was the victory of cowries.

In the next moment he thought, “But what is the value of a cowrie?” He had just six pockets, four on his coat and two in his trousers. Even if he filled all six pockets with cowries, they wouldnʼt be of much value.

Kipt́ekaiṋjus rejected the cowries and moved on. After walking some distance, he saw another hill in front of him. It was a hill of copper [táṋbá ( 3 ) ] coins. Kiptekainjus thought that although copper coins are much more valuable than cowries, even then, six pocketfuls of copper coins would not make him really a rich man. So he crossed the copper hill and moved on.
After walking farther he saw a hill of silver [rúpo ( 4 )] coins before him.

Kipt́ekaiṋjus felt that to fill his six pockets with silver coins involved three problems. First, the total value of the silver coins was not so much. Secondly, he would not be able to walk fast on account of the weight of the silver coins. Thirdly, the coins would make a clanking sound and this would give the impression to thieves and dacoits that he had a lot of money.

In those days, there was no Rs.1 currency note. In the British period, the use of cowries was banned. Coins made of copper, bronze, or silver were mostly in use. (Gold coins with alloy, which are called sovereigns in English and gini in Bengali, from which we have the word ginisońá, were also used, though they were scarce.) That is why the shopkeepers, when going home from their shops, used to put their coins in a bundle and tightly tie them up so that they did not make any noise. The bundle of even a small merchant usually contained a large number of coins.

While talking about the merchantsʼ bundles, I remember a story of those days. Once, a guru went on a round of the houses of his disciples to collect money. It was wintertime, just after harvesting, the most appropriate time for collecting money. In honour of the guruʼs visit, the disciples gave him a warm reception and delicious treats. At this time, a particular disciple had a lot of money. At night, he asked his guru, “Master, itʼs winter now. Will you use a blanket or a quilt at night? I have both ready for you.” The guru thought, “Let me pretend to be a god-man this time.”

Once upon a time, a few dead crows were lying scattered about the hermitage of a fakir [a Muslim ascetic]. People asked him, “Fakir Saheb, why did so many forest crows die in the storm?” The Fakir replied, “The crows used to disturb me a lot. Yesterday evening I strongly warned them. I said to them, ‘f you donʼt behave properly I will finish you all offʼ. Just see, before a single night had passed, they all were struck dead by the storm. Had they followed my instruction and learnt to cuckoo instead of cawing, they would not have suffered such a fate.”

The guru realized that the crows had died naturally in a storm, yet the credit had gone to the fakir. Thus, there is a Bengali proverb – jhaŕe kák mare phakirer kyáramatii báŕe [The crows die in a storm and the fakir gets the credit]. The guru thought, “Let me also show my charisma in the house of this disciple of mine.”
He told his disciple, “Look, we are all great men. We donʼt feel hot or cold, so there is no need of the quilt or the blanket.”

After dinner, the guru went to his room. The disciple was a very good person. He kept sitting at the door with a blanket wrapped around him, so that if his guru should feel cold, he could immediately give him a quilt or a blanket. He saw, through a chink in the door, that in the first part of the night his guru was lying straight, with his hands and legs outstretched. He said to himself, “In the first part of the night my master is an incarnation of a d́heṋki [a kind of husking pedal operated in a seesaw manner]. In the second part of the night, the guru started feeling cold and he drew up his knees. The disciple outside broke into a song, “In the second part of the night my master is a stringed bow.” During the third part of the night it became colder, and the body of the guru also shrank in cold. The disciple sang, “In the third part of the night my master is curled up like a dog”. In the fourth part of the night, as it became very cold, the body of the guru looked almost like a circle. On seeing this, the disciple sang, “In the fourth part of the night, my master is a merchantʼs bundle.” However, we return to the point that Kipt́ekaiṋjus did not want to move around with a merchantʼs bundle.

He moved forward. Kipt́ekaiṋjus moved on and on for days and months. He passed many sleepless nights and was drenched many times by rain, but Kipt́ekaiṋjus did not care about any of this. His sole aim was to collect wealth, and his mind kept on whispering, “I am hungry, I am hungry.”
Suddenly, he noticed a hill of glittering gold [sońá ( 5 )] surrounding him on all sides. It was made of gold coins, which were called siinaka in ancient times.

On seeing the hill of gold, Kipt́ekaiṋjus was simply dazzled. He thought, “Oh God, at last my lifelong wish of this life and many previous lives is finally fulfilled. Today I am the richest person, but how shall I carry all this wealth home? Where shall I keep it? I shall further increase my wealth through interest accrued on it. Until now, I used to have only muŕi [puffed rice] with oil, salt and green chilli for my breakfast. From now on, I shall leave out the chillies and eat only dry muŕi to reduce my expenditure. I must increase my income, but the final problem is how to carry this wealth home? This hill of gold cannot be stuffed into my six pockets.”

Kipt́ekaiṋjus thought, “Let me move farther on and see what is in store for me.” Kiptekainjus started running fast like a horse – like a horse without reins – at a meteoric speed. After going some distance he saw that there was a hill of precious stones [mańi] – gems, pearls and jewels. He could easily buy a hill of gold with a handful of those gems and jewels.

He thought, “Since I have come this far, let me move a little farther on and see if I can get something more valuable.” He kept on running, with tired limbs and almost out of breath. He started sweating all over and even then he went on running and running. Was there no end to this running?

After covering some distance, he saw that a brahmadatyi [brahmadaetya] [a man-eating ghost of a Brahman] was standing in the middle of the road, and a huge wheel with very sharp blades was rotating on his head. His head was cut open by the wheel so that the soft grey matter of his brain was coming out and he was bleeding profusely. The brahmadaitya was crying at the top of his lungs: “Oh, I am undone. Alas, I am undone, I am dying, please save me, I donʼt want money, I donʼt want wealth, I only want peace, I want that peace which is the greatest wealth of life!” The drops of blood spilling out of the brahmadaityaʼs head were scattering about on all sides, and from every drop of blood was born an extremely greedy person. These people, quarreling and fighting amongst themselves, grovelled in the dust until they died. The last particle of their existence was lost in the bottomless abyss of darkness.

Kipt́ekaiṋjus asked the brahmadaitya, “My dear brother, why is that rotating wheel on your head? How come cakraḿ bhramati mastake [that wheel is rotating on your head] endlessly?” As soon as Kipt́ekaiṋjus uttered these words, the wheel left the brahmadaityaʼs head, landed on his own head and started rotating very fast. Kiptekainjus cried out in excruciating agony, “I donʼt want wealth, I have been going on the wrong path. I donʼt want Kuberʼs wealth through Shivaʼs recommendation. I want peace, the profound peace that is ensconced in Shiva. Please save me, whoever is around, please save me, I am undone, I am dying! Is there nobody to save me? I want only Shiva, Shiva smeared with ashes.”

The brahmadaitya said, “I was also extremely greedy and a victim of attachment, like you. I also arrived here just as you did. On reaching here I saw that a wheel was rotating on the head of a brahmapisháca. I also asked him, ”Well, brother, why is a wheel rotating on your head?“ The arrangement, as decided by Lord Shiva, is that this is the final outcome of attachment: Cakraḿ bhramati mastake. If some other person, as greedy as you, comes and asks you, 'My dear brother, why is that wheel rotating on your head?ʼ the wheel will immediately move onto his head, and you will be relieved from its oppression. Well, brother, I am off. I donʼt know how long I was in the condition of cakraḿ bhrumarti mastake. I must return now.”

The brahmadaitya further said, “The bel ( 6 ) [the marmelos aegle, the wood apple] tree under which I took shelter on becoming a brahmadaitya must have died by now, after such a long time. So I must look for another new bel tree for my shelter.
When you become liberated by the grace of Lord Shiva, then come under my bel tree. I will bring you up into the tree with the help of a ladder.”

Kipt́ekaiṋjus kept on standing there all alone. Blood started dripping down his head and the drops of blood were being scattered all over the world. From every drop of blood were born greedy monsters, prisoners of attachment. Kipt́ekaiṋjus was crying at the top of his lungs, “Alas I am undone, I am dying, cakraḿ bhamati mastake.”

So, now you understand the consequences of attachment as a ripu [enemy]. By and large, bondages such as hatred and fear are actually born out of this ripu of attachment. The only way to escape this is to think about the Supreme Being. There is no other way out; nányah panthá vidyate ayanáya [There is no way other than this].

As it is not desirable to translate a proper noun, similarly, it is desirable to retain its pronunciation. It is not desirable to make the slightest exception in any of these cases. In other words, a proper noun should be pronounced properly, and while using it or addressing a person it must not be translated.
My friend Sardar Hajara Singh was going to England. I told him, “Learn some English. You donʼt have to read Milton or Shakespeare, just a working knowledge of English will do.”
He said, “Yes, I am just learning like that.” After sometime he told me, “The day after tomorrow I am leaving for England.”
I said to him, “I hope you are now reasonably proficient in English.”
He said, “Yes, sir.”
I asked, “If somebody asks you, ‘Whatʼs your name?ʼ what will you say?”

He said, “I shall say: Liid́ár thaujyáńd́á láyan. Our English teacher taught us that sardár is liid́ár [leader] in English and hájár is tháujyáńd́ [thousand] in English. But my name is not hájár but hájárá. So I made it tháujyáńd́á . And the English for Singh is láyan [lion]. So in English my name is Liid́ár tháujyańd́á láyan.”

An enlightened human, resplendent with the brilliance of wisdom, was never so since the moment of his or her birth. Enlightenment and rationality free from dogmatic ideas come step by step at a certain stage of the rhythmic movement of the development of human consciousness through various impediments and constraints. I cannot say that the humans of today have become completely free from dogmas. In fact, the humans of today are yet to become free from superstitions. This is the reason why there are so many clashes, murders, quarrels, squabbles and misunderstandings among humans. Those who give the excuse of misunderstanding usually deliberately misunderstand or pretend to misunderstand in order to fulfill their own interests. Yet, the wisdom of the humans of earlier times must certainly have been less profound than that of the humans of today. Their lives were based on blind attachment to dogmas. Those superstitions of theirs, continuing for such a long time, have done a great injury to a large part of society, making it suffer the cataclysmic crisis of decadence. Those people who tried to control this decadence either died out, or somehow survived and trudged on with broken knees. The idea of the yakśa was one such superstition born out of dogmatic beliefs.

In ancient times, avaricious people thought that if they buried their wealth deep in the ground and engaged a yakśa to look after it, that yakśa would guard their wealth for a long time, until the appearance of the rightful owner, to whom it would hand over the wealth and be liberated.

A yakśa [was considered to be] an assistant of Kuber [the god of wealth], so it would never allow wealth to go to waste. On the strength of this belief, people would build a small room under the earth, in which to keep their wealth. They would seat a young, dark-skinned boy there, in front of a lighted lamp, and perform some occult rites (this type of negative occult ritual is called pha). Then, on coming back above ground, they would cover the roof of that room with earth, camouflaging it with the adjoining land so that nobody would suspect anything from outside. After sometime, the flame of the lamp would go out, and simultaneously, the lamp of that innocent boyʼs life would also be extinguished. He would fall into an eternal slumber in the abyss of darkness.

People believed that the boy would turn into a yakśa and that he would guard the wealth. They thought that he would be freed only after he had handed over the entire wealth to the rightful owner at the appropriate time. In Bengali, this type of wealth was called yakher dhan in common speech. In Bihar, the places which were known to have such wealth were called brhamasthán [the seat of Brahma]. Even today, one can find such brahmastháns under a huge banyan tree or a pipul tree [Ficus religiosa] outside the villages. Nobody likes to go to such places – in fact, people are afraid to go to such places after sunset.

Not only those innocent boys but also young, innocent dark-skinned girls were subjected to the atrocities of the superstitious process of making a yakśa. A wealthy man would dig a huge tank and keep his wealth at the bottom of it. A young, dark-skinned girl would have her hands and legs tied, and would be drowned in that tank, while occult rituals were performed (needless to say, this was also called pha). The moment the dead body of the girl surfaced, it was presumed that the dead girl had turned into a yakśińii [a female yakśa]. It was believed that when the rightful owner of that wealth would come to that tank in future, the yakśińii would hand over the wealth to him, and she would then become free. Such a yakśińii used to be called yakhe buŕii in the Bengali vernacular of that time. A tank where such macabre rituals were performed was called yakher pukur [a yakśaʼs tank] or tálpukur [a tank with palm trees]. Some people think that if the water in a tank is deep (tál is a measure of water, such as báṋo), then that tank is called a tálpukur. This is not wholly true. Palm trees were planted around a tank just to mislead people. There is a prevalent notion that in the event of a sudden need of a large number of utensils on account of some feast or yajiṋa [an elaborate worship], if a girl goes to that tank, stands in the neck-deep water and prays to the yakhe buŕii, then the following morning, the yakhe buŕii will supply the utensils and leave them on the bank of the tank. After the ceremonial function is over it is necessary to return the utensils after washing them clean, and leaving them on the bank of the tank. It is believed that if some greedy person steals those utensils, the yakhe buŕii will catch hold of their legs and drag them down to hell when they come to the tank again in future.
So, you have heard the story of yakhe buŕii. Just imagine the kind of superstitions that prevailed those days.

While talking about yakher dhan and yakhe buŕii, I remember Bhuṋŕobhombal Bhar. He lived in Bhoṋdaŕpur, near Bhadreshvar. For breakfast he used to buy one pice worth of pyáṋj phulurii [a kind of vegetable chop made of powdered pigeon-peas and onions] in the morning, and would eat this four times a day for refreshment. Bhuṋŕobhombal had a huge property, a huge collection of dazzling gems and jewels, such as diamonds, sapphires and many other precious stones. Bhuṋŕobhombal worried what would happen if his descendents squandered his enormous wealth. What would happen if they wasted all his things? In that case he would not find peace even after death.

Báburám Bhar was his only son. You know the functions of five generations in regard to wealth. The first generation only buys property and collects wealth. So it may be called Kenárám [the buying generation]. The second generation enjoys the property, spends it in luxury and swaggers about in aristocratic style. It may be called Báburám [the luxurious generation]. The third generation maintains the same luxurious habits by selling the property. It may be called Becárám [the selling generation]. During the selling generation, the property practically becomes completely exhausted, and as a result the next generation spends its days in great hardship. So it may be called Dukhiirám [the suffering generation]. After Duhkhiirám, there is practically no property left, so the fifth generation takes to begging for a living. This may be called Bhikhurám [the begging generation]. So our Bhuṋŕobhombal was Kenárám and his only son was Báburám.

On account of his extravagant habits, Baburam fell under the wrath of Bhuṋŕobhombal. One day, he gave his son a good thrashing with a stick and drove him out of the house. The son started living in a different village, spending his days in misery. Bhuṋŕobhombal was now beside himself with joy. He was happy that his money had completely stopped draining away.

For his lunch and dinner, Bhuṋŕobhombal used to have newly harvested aush rice [rice made from paddy which ripens in the rainy season or autumn] with rice water. The new aush rice takes time to digest, so a little quantity fills the stomach. People used to ask him, “Why donʼt you strain the water from the rice?” He used to reply, “Doctors say that the water contains vitamins.” He used to eat burnt brinjals with boiled rice, because compared to fried brinjal, burnt brinjal needs very little oil, so little, in fact, that it can be burnt even without using any oil. He used to collect jujubes that had fallen from the tree, prepare a sour curry with them and eat it. When jujubes were not available he used to buy a few hog plums or tamarind and prepare a sour sauce, and felt very unhappy that he had to incur an additional expenditure. He felt uneasy during the day and could not sleep at night. After the expulsion of his son his expenditure was considerably reduced.

One day, he thought, “Who knows into whose extravagant hands my huge property will fall after my death?” He decided to bury his wealth under the ground and hand it over to a yakh [yakśa]. He thought that the yakh would hand over that wealth to the rightful heir or he would take it back from the yakh when he was reborn as a human being in his next birth. He did not look for a mason to construct the underground room in which to keep the wealth meant for the yakh. There were two reasons for this. The first and foremost reason was that the mason in that case would come to know about the hidden wealth. And the second reason was that it had often happened that cruel people had murdered the mason after their underground room had been constructed, so that the secret would not leak out. Once these crimes became public knowledge, masons were not willing to build underground rooms for hiding wealth. So Bhuṋŕobhombal started building the room himself with various necessary implements and building materials. It is not an easy job to make a room underground.

After some time, the room was finished. Bhuṋŕobhombal also took lessons from a negative occultist in the rituals to be performed for making a yakśa. However, it was difficult to find a young, dark-skinned boy. He avidly waited, like the crow of a sacred place, for a such a boy to come in the direction of his house, by chance. Even the beggar boys never came near his house because he never gave any alms. On the contrary, instead of getting alms they got a beating. One day, he saw that a dark-skinned boy of about five years old was passing by his house. He was wearing silver bangles. In Bengal, in those days, both men and women used to wear bangles. Both the children of well-to-do families as well as those of ordinary families used to wear golden bangles, while the poor ones used to wear bangles made of silver or bell metal. On seeing the boyʼs silver bangles, Bhuṋŕobhombal understood that the boy belonged to a poor family. He then tempted the boy with a treat of sweets and brought him within the compound of his house. Then he led him to the underground room, and lighting a lamp before him, started performing the occult rituals. We have already said that such a ritual is pha. The lamp was burning, flickering, and intermittently blazing up rather tremulously. The boy became afraid and wanted to go away. He started imploring and crying to be let go. But the impervious heart of Bhuṋŕobhombal did not melt. He left the boy there, and covered the room by spreading earth over it. Certainly, the lamp became extinguished after sometime, and the lamp of that boyʼs life was also extinguished forever. Bhuṋŕobhombal, full of joy, went back to his house. He was happy that at last a solution had been found for preserving his huge property. Today, fully satisfied, he would eat stale rice with a curry made of potato skins, then have a deep sleep.

But could he really sleep? As he was lying down he heard the dark-skinned boy mumbling into his right ear, “Please let me go, let me go home.” As it became unbearable, he plugged his right ear. But then he started hearing the boy mumbling into his left ear, “Please let me go, my mother will cry for me.” He plugged both his ears. Then he started seeing a nightmare in front of his eyes. He saw that the little boy was crying, pleading, “I am certainly not a bad boy. Then why are you killing me? Donʼt you know that my father will go about looking for me everywhere?”

Bhuṋŕobhombal then shut both his eyes. But then it flashed in his mindʼs eye that the dark-skinned boy was crying and saying, “Both my parents love me dearly. If I die they will cry inconsolably. Please donʼt kill me.”
Bhuṋŕobhombal spent a sleepless night. He was perplexed, dazed, tired and lost.

The next morning he saw that, after many long years, his son Báburám was coming towards his house. His hair was disheveled, his face was worried and his eyes were full of anxiety. Bhuṋŕobhombal thought that Báburám must have come to ask for money. Before his son could come close to him, he snubbed him, “Why have you come again, and with what motive? I havenʼt got any money, and even if I had, I wouldnʼt give you any.”
Báburám said, “Oh, no, I havenʼt come for money. Our son has been missing since yesterday. So I just came to see if he came this way.”
Bhuṋŕobhombal said, “I have never seen the boy. How old is he? What does he look like?”
Báburám said, “He is about five years old and has a dark complexion. He has silver bangles on his wrists, as our family is poor.”
Bhuṋŕobhombal started shouting and tearing his hair and broke down in tears. He said, “Just yesterday I turned him into a yakh. Oh, what have I done! Nobody is now left to continue my line!”
Báburám said, “Tell me where you buried him. I have to take back the body of my boy because I need to perform his last rites.”

Bhuṋŕobhombal pointed to the place and said, “The child is in his eternal sleep there. Just by his side is lying the huge wealth of Kuber. Take away your boy for his last rites and take along all that wealth as well.”

Báburám said, “I will definitely take away the body because the last rites have to be performed but that Kuberʼs wealth I wonʼt touch. You may turn into a yakśa and guard that yakher dhan life after life.”

Báburám collected the dead body of his son, took it in his arms, and went away, weeping. The numbed, drooping hands of the boy were hanging loosely, with a pair of bangles on them. After all, he was the son of a poor man! So he wore silver bangles. Bhuṋŕobhombal, unable to stand the intolerable mental pressure, succumbed to death.

What is Bhuṋŕobhombal doing now? Is he guarding the yakher dhan, after turning into a yakśa? But he has no descendant. No claimant will liberate him in future. Will he then continue the life of a yakśa eternally? But alas, with his own hands he has sealed the path of his freedom with molten steel for eternity!
